# PREFACE.

<image-desc>Large ornate decorative initial 'S' at the beginning of the text, featuring detailed scrollwork and foliage patterns within a square border.</image-desc>The Philosopher <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts</note>, the prince of philosophers, writes: Man is the best of all things that are in the world. Here, "the world" is understood to include everything contained within the sphere of active and passive things—namely, the elements <note>earth, air, fire, and water</note> and things composed of elements. With this presupposed, the proposition is proven: That thing is best whose causes of generation are most noble; but such is the case for man, therefore he is the best. The major premise is evident, because an effect derives its nobility from its causes. The minor premise is proven regarding the matter of man. Wherefore, the matter of man, according to the Physicians, is posited to be the menstrual blood of the woman together with the seed of the man, because both of these enter into the composition of man, just as milk is curdled into the substance of cheese. But the material Philosophers posit that the woman's menstrual blood is the matter, and the man's seed is the efficient cause <note>the agent that brings about change</note>, such that the man's seed relates to the woman's menstrual blood as the craftsman relates to the craft, as Averroes <note>The influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle</note> attests in the 7th book of the *Metaphysics*, in the Digressions on Ideas. Likewise, the Philosopher in the 5th book of the *Metaphysics*, chapter 10, says that the seed of the man is reduced to the efficient cause. Whichever way it is said, it is always evident that the matter of man is most excellent, and the most noble among all seeds.

Secondly, it is proven: that thing is best which, in its parts, is assimilated to the most noble body; but man is of this kind, therefore he is the best. The major premise is evident, because assimilation follows the nature of the thing. The minor premise is proven because man is assimilated to the heavens, specifically to the twelve signs of the zodiac. Three of these are virtually hot, namely Aries, Gemini, and Leo; to these correspond three members in man: the heart, the liver, and the testicles. Likewise, three are cold: Cancer, Taurus, and Virgo; to these correspond the intestines, the bladder, and the diaphragm. Likewise, three are moist: Scorpio, Aquarius, and Pisces; to these correspond the brain, the stomach, and the lungs. Likewise, three are dry: Capricorn, Sagittarius, and Libra; to these correspond the spleen, the gall <note>the gallbladder or bile</note>,

...and the kidneys. Whence it is said in the 12th book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle’s work on the nature of existence and the divine</note> that the whole heaven is like a single contiguous composite; therefore, we ought to be inclined toward the knowledge of the present book, which treats of human generation. Its efficient cause <note>The agent or author responsible for bringing the work into being</note> is said to have been Albertus Magnus <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a famous scholar and bishop</note>, with most parts taken from Aristotle, who was sufficiently practiced or learned in experiments and informed by women. This is especially true in his *Book on Animals*, which he composed after traveling the whole world with Alexander <note>Alexander the Great, Aristotle's famous pupil</note>. This work is categorized under natural philosophy, because it is one of the books on "small natural matters" <note>original: "parvis naturalibus," referring to the *Parva Naturalia*, a collection of short treatises by Aristotle on nature and psychology</note>, and it is not purely natural philosophy, but partly medicinal.

# P R E F A C E

To his beloved companion and friend in Christ, N., a cleric of such-and-such a place: true wisdom, and the continuous increase of the present life.

The subject of this book is "mobile being" <note>A standard Scholastic term for physical matter subject to change</note>, narrowed down to the nature of the secrets of women, so that when they are ill, we may be able to provide remedies; and when they are confessing, we may know how to give penances appropriate to the offense. It is divided first into two parts, *namely the introductory and the executive. The executive part begins there, "as it is written," etc.* First, the author greets the person to whom he writes, saying: *I, Albert, dwelling in Paris, to his beloved companion and friend in Christ.* Here the *efficient cause* is touched upon, both *moving* and *moved*. The *moving cause* was a certain priest, who asked Lord Albert to write him a book on the secrets of women. And this was because women are poisonous at the time of their menses, so much so that they intoxicate animals by their gaze, infect children in their cradles, stain a well-polished mirror, and sometimes cause one having intercourse with them to become leprous or cancerous. And because evil is not avoided unless it is known: therefore it is necessary for those wishing to abstain to know the uncleanness of coitus, and many other things which are taught in this book. And so Albert, seeing that he asked justly, consented to him, and thus the *efficient cause* is touched upon; and the *moved cause* when it is said, *I write, etc. Wisdom is the knowledge of God and of eternal effects.* And therefore the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the preface to the *Metaphysics*: *Of God properly it is not...*

# Preface

->Introduction<-

Knowledge is a great thing. Nothing is better in this life, because through it we are made happy, as Averroës <note>Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to medieval science.</note> testifies in the prologue to the fourth book of *Physics*. Therefore, the author writes for the improvement of the present life, and he writes these things well for himself, because through wisdom, a man is rendered praiseworthy to God and to men.

When your favorable and gracious company asked me to more clearly reveal certain things which are hidden and secret regarding the nature and condition of women, having seen your petition, no laziness held me back from compiling a brief and concise little treatise once the material was obtained. But my small and youthful mind, which is drawn to other things according to its possibility and the opportunity of the time, nevertheless desiring to satisfy your appetite, I write to you this present letter. In it, you will find many things concerning what has been requested, written partly in a philosophical style and partly in a medicinal style, as seems appropriate to the subject matter. I have written this asking for your constancy, that you be steadfast and secretive in this work and business, and that you do not permit any boy—whether in age or in behavior—to come into its presence. If you do this, I promise to reveal more to you about these and other matters, and to transmit them with the present work and art for medicinal reasons, which I shall give more at length, the Lord permitting.

*Here he shows the cause which could excuse him from the labor of this deed, and the meaning is clear from the text. Note that the author says that a youthful and small mind held him back, whereby he avoids arrogance; for a mind is called "small" when it is imbued with small conditions of knowledge. Hence the intellect is not properly small in itself, nor by accident, because the intellect is not extended by expansion nor by reduction. Note that appetite is twofold, namely natural and intellectual. Regarding the purpose, the text says "to the appetite," glossed as: "that is, to the natural intellect." Hence that priest <note>The commentator here identifies the seeker as a priest or cleric.</note> desired by natural appetite to know the natures of women. For men by nature desire to know, as stated in the first book of the Metaphysics <note>Aristotle's Metaphysics, Book I.</note>. Likewise, he desired it by intellectual appetite, because he saw the utility of knowing them.*

As it is written in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals* <note>Aristotle's work on biology and reproduction.</note>, generation is an eternal cycle. Moreover, the cause of eternity in the generation of ani—

# Preface

...of animals, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> shows in the second book of *On the Soul*, saying: "The most natural of works is for each thing to generate another like itself, so that they may participate in the divine and immortal being; for all things desire this so that they may remain—not as the same individual in number, but as the same in species." For this reason, the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> says in the second book of *On the Soul* that because divine providence <note>original: "sollicitudo divina"</note> could not make the individual human being remain the same in number, it took pity on him by giving him the power by which he could remain the same in species. And he adds: "For there is no doubt that it is better to have this power than not to have it, or not to exist at all."

*This is the executive part in which the author pursues his intent by putting forward two propositions serving his purpose. It is divided into as many chapters and parts as will appear in order. Note: the generation of perfect animals is eternal, because such things belong to the universal perfection of the world, according to the first book of the Ethics. But a doubt seems to arise, because certain animals are at times entirely destroyed, such as certain worms and flies in winter. It must be said that if they are destroyed in one climate, they are then generated in another, according to Albert <note>Albertus Magnus</note> and in the commentary on the first book of the Posterior Analytics. Or it must be said that the generation of animals is eternal because they belong to the universal perfection; but if the first solution stands, it is doubtful whether those animals belong to the universal perfection, because it would be better for many animals not to exist than to exist—namely snakes and animals that are poisonous. It is said that it is good for them to exist so that they may absorb the impurities of the earth; for if they did not absorb them, they would infect the air, and consequently, man. Hence, nature displays nothing without a reasonable cause. From that text, it is clear that chastity is a sin against nature—although for men it is a way of death by the precept of the law—because through chastity an animal does not generate its like. Note: by "divine providence" one cannot understand God Himself, because He does not care for particulars according to Averroes in the twelfth book of the Metaphysics; therefore, by divine providence is understood the celestial body, which by its own nature and natural appetite desires to preserve these lower things, though mediated by the governance of the Intelligences <note>The spiritual beings or "angels" believed to move the celestial spheres</note>. Hence the Commentator in the twelfth book of the Metaphysics says: "The work of nature is the work of an Intelligence that does not err." Can the generation of animals preserve animals in their specific being forever? It is said no, because if so, the species would be capable of being generated <note>i.e., having a beginning in time</note>, which is false:*

# Preface

...the falsehood is clear, because the species is perpetual <note>original: "species est perpetua"; the idea that while individuals die, the category or "kind" (species) exists forever in nature.</note>. I say that when this or that individual is generated, the specific nature is then generated under this designated being and in part, even though it is not generated according to its entire scope. For this reason, note that nature works secretly in universals <note>A "universal" is a general concept, like "humanity," as opposed to a "particular" like a specific person.</note>, as **Gilbert Porretanus** <note>Gilbert de la Porrée (c. 1070–1154), a famous scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> says in his *Six Principles* in the first chapter (specifically the chapter on form). And because nature intends to produce a "manly nature"—that is, humanity in general, or the horse—and yet it produces a particular individual, such as a strong man, this happens because it finds certain matter designated in this specific place. Therefore, if it found all of nature at once, it would produce every human at once; but because it finds only a portion of the menstrual fluid <note>Medieval biology held that the mother's menstrual blood provided the material substance for the child's body.</note> of this or that woman, it therefore produces this particular human.

The reason why these animals, and especially humans, do not endure according to the same nature, matter, and number is stated in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption* <note>A treatise by Aristotle on how things are born and how they decay.</note>. Things whose bodily substance does not endure, but is corruptible, could not repeat as the same individuals in number. But because the substance of a human, taken according to the principles of the individual, is corruptible, the individual generation of a human is cast aside <note>Meaning the individual passes away to make room for the next.</note>; for which reason the generation of humans will not be eternal in number. Nevertheless, the generation of humans is the most perfect. This is proved thus: because man is the noblest creature, which is clear from the intention of the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> in many places, and especially in the second book of *On the Soul*. For the more operations <note>Actions or functions.</note> a thing has, the nobler it is; and man is separated from the number of other living things by his intellectual reason, as is clear in that same text.

This is also the intention of all the Philosophers, especially **Boethius** in the second book of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, where he says that humans are like God in their mind. This is also clear in these matters because motion takes its nature and species from its goal <term>terminus ad quem<gloss>The "end point" or final destination of a process of change.</gloss></term>. Therefore, since human nature comes to exist in Socrates or Plato, or in any other particular existing human, the motion which is called "generation" becomes most perfect; it will be the most perfect among the generation of all animals. Furthermore, generation is a motion from non-being to being. Now, "being" is what is most greatly desired; and especially by humans, because here among all mo...

# Preface

...[the spirit] is excellent in its mobility. And understand this regarding a motion that changes something upon which it moves; by this, the primary motion—which is the cause of all others—is excluded <note>The "primary motion" usually refers to the movement of the highest celestial sphere, which medieval philosophers believed drove all other changes in the universe.</note>.

*Here he proves that animals cannot remain the same in number <note>To be "the same in number" (unum numero) means to be the exact same individual being, rather than just a member of the same group.</note>, but certainly the same in species, and especially humans. It is doubted whether the same individual, having been destroyed in number, can be regenerated? And it seems that yes, because after thirty-seven thousand years, the constellation of the heaven will be the same throughout, just as it is now, according to Plato and the Astronomers. And therefore we will then be the same in number, and we will sit in this or that school or lecture hall, just as we do now—namely, in the "Great Year" <note>original: "magno anno"; the period of time it takes for all the planets and stars to return to the same relative positions.</note>. Hence Plato said that after the Great Year he must return to Athens and must read there: the reason is that the entire constellation will happen in just that way. Therefore, when the same constellation returns, the same effects will return.*

*This is spoken according to the opinion of **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a Spanish-Muslim philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were fundamental to medieval university education.</note> and **Aristotle** in the fifth book of the **Physics** and in the book **On Generation**: it is not possible because the generations and destructions of that person could not then be immediate; therefore time would come between them. And thus, something that is "one in number" is lost by a single change, according to the fifth book of the **Physics**. But regarding the first doubt, it must be said that after the Great Year it is possible for men to return who are very similar, so much so that they can hardly be recognized as distinct, although they are not the same in number. But you might say: if the same cause of matter remains, the effect will be the same in number. It is answered that this is true if the same measure and equally disposed matter remain, but it is not so, because time passes rapidly and does not return as the same in number, though certainly the same in species. And it can be said that today's resolution <note>original: "resolutio"; the breaking down or dissolution of bodily matter back into its elements.</note> is not the same in number as the resolution which comes after a thousand or four hundred years, since motion is a successive being.*

*It is doubted secondly, whether one animal can be perpetuated forever? And it seems so, because it is possible to find some "complexed" thing <note>A "complexion" refers to the specific mixture of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) and qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in a body.</note> in which the elements are reduced to a mean or a middle proportion; because all destruction comes from a "contrary," and if those contraries are balanced at the highest level, they are not destroyed. But that this is possible is proved thus: because where there is a "greater equal," there is equality simply. I say that it is not possible to grant this: that which is mixed is moved by the nature of the predominant element, that is, the heaven. But to the reasoning "where there is a greater equal and lesser," etc.: respond that it is true insofar as the equal suffices and insofar as it is possible. Thus the mixture...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of existence and generation, transitioning from the celestial "Great Year" to the physical composition of living beings and the philosophical nobility of human life.</meta>

# Preface

...an equality in humors must be established according to a proper balance <note>original: "secundum justitiam"; in this context, "justice" refers to a proportional balance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—rather than legal justice.</note>, but it is not possible to grant an equality according to the quantity of the matter, because earth always predominates in most mixtures. Stated another way: even supposing that such a mixture were so perfectly weighted in every quality of the elements, it would still be subject to decay from the outside, namely by celestial power. For it could be cooled by means of cold water, and thus return to a state of imbalance—leaving that equality of humors—and in this way be destroyed.

Note that the text says humans are like God in mind; this is evident because a person becomes divine through knowledge. **Seneca** <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), a Stoic philosopher.</note> says a contemplative man is like God and most beloved by Him. This is also clear from the second book of the **Metaphysics** <note>A foundational work by Aristotle on the nature of reality.</note> where **Aristotle** says that in humans there is pleasure for a short time, through which, by their intelligence, they perfect the whole inner self. And he understands by this the knowledge of God, in which there is the greatest pleasure.

Note that all pleasure happens through a certain likeness or assimilation of the knower to the thing known, by means of the "exemplary form" <note>A mental pattern or blueprint that allows the mind to recognize and connect with an object.</note> of the knower. Therefore, the more a human knows about God, the more or more greatly he is made like Him.

The text says that among all movements, **generation** <note>The process of coming into being or being born.</note> is the most noble. Taking this to mean the drawing forth of the soul or the formation of the fetus in the womb—how this may be a movement will be seen.

Regarding this, note that movement is twofold. One is a movement that casts something off from the substance, just as the heating of water casts off coldness, or as a color moves from white to blackness. The other is a movement that does not cast off any perfection from the substance of the movement; such is the motion of the heavens, which does not cause anything to be destroyed from the substance of the sky.

Now, generation is a movement that casts something off from the substance of a thing, because the menstrual material <note>original: "menstruum"; in medieval embryology, based on Aristotle, the mother was thought to provide the physical matter for the fetus from menstrual blood, while the father provided the "form" or life-force.</note> which is moved toward the formation of a human is transformed. Hence **Averroes** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century Islamic philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> says in the first book of the **Physics**: "In the generation of a human, part of the seed <note>original: "spermatis"; used here generally for the reproductive matter.</note> does not cease being destroyed, and part of the human is generated, until the whole form is completed."

->ON THE GENERATION OF THE *EMBRYO.*<-

### CHAPTER ONE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'P' with ornate floral and foliate scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>
After our previous discourse has addressed those matters which incline the listener's attention toward the subject of our writing, it is now appropriate to descend into the actual substance of the work: and first, to examine the generation of the embryo. In accordance with this, it must be noted diligently and committed to memory that every human who is naturally conceived is generated from the father's seed and the mother's menses <note>original: "menstruo"; in medieval embryology, the "menstruum" was often viewed as the female equivalent of seed or the raw material from which the fetus was fashioned.</note>, according to the consensus of all Philosophers and Physicians. And I specify "Physicians" because **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), the Greek philosopher whose theories on "form" and "matter" shaped medieval science.</note> did not propose that the father's seed becomes part of the physical substance of the fetus; rather, he says the fetus proceeds only from the menses, and afterward, he posits that the paternal seed evaporates away like a vapor. Physicians, however, say that the entire seed—both from the father (which is called sperm <term>sperma: the male reproductive fluid</term>) and from the mother (which is called the menses <term>menstruum: here used to denote the female's material contribution to conception</term>)—combines to form the physical substance of the fetus.

*Chapter of the first practical part, in which he intends to approach the subject matter, namely to demonstrate the generation of the embryo or fetus. There is no controversy between Physicians and Philosophers regarding the basic components. For the philosophers say that the seed of the man, joined with the menses of the woman, relates to the woman's menses as a craftsman relates to his craft. Thus, just as a Carpenter is solely the efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into being, like the builder of a house.</note> and the house is the effect—meaning he transforms the material of the house—*

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

<summary>This page introduces the biological study of human conception, contrasting the Aristotelian view (that the father provides only the "form" or "spirit") with the medical view (that both parents contribute physical substance to the embryo).</summary>
<keywords>embryology, conception, Aristotle, sperm, menses, efficient cause, fetal development, medieval medicine</keywords>

# ON THE SECRETS OF WOMEN.

...and disposes [the matter]; likewise, the male sperm alters the woman’s menses <note>original: "menstruum"; in this context, the maternal contribution to the physical substance of the child.</note> into the form of a human being. They [the Philosophers] propose this because they observe that when the father’s contribution is "corrupted" <note>original: "corrupto"; in medieval Aristotelian physics, "corruption" does not mean "rot," but rather the transformation or dissolution of one thing so that another—the generation of the fetus—can begin.</note>, the generation of a human occurs through the transformation of the woman’s seed. Therefore, one must posit an **efficient cause** whereby, once the father’s seed is transformed, the woman’s menses are changed. And because the final purpose and the physical effect coincide, the male sperm does not actually become part of the material substance. 

But the **Physicians** argue the opposite: namely, that a human being is formed from the most noble matter. Therefore, although the seed entering the matter of the female fetus is a surplus of the **second digestion** <term>second digestion: the stage of the medieval digestive process where nutrients are converted into blood and bodily fluids</term>, the male sperm is more perfectly "cooked" <note>Ancient and medieval medicine viewed the creation of bodily fluids as a process of "coction" or ripening by heat.</note> and digested. Thus, it must enter into the very matter and substance of the fetus, for it is observed that a fetus sometimes resembles the father in the genitals and many other features; this would not occur unless the sperm entered the fetus’s physical substance. 

Furthermore, the Physicians say that within the male seed there exists a certain **generative spirit** <term>spiritus gignens: a vital, formative force believed to animate matter.</term> that penetrates the entire mass of the joined seeds. This spirit is the formatter of all the limbs: just as a blacksmith shapes iron with a hammer, so does this spirit shape and soften all the limbs, and through this spirit, the active **efficient principle** is maintained. 

However, the **Philosophers** maintain that the male sperm evaporates like a vapor, because the womb <term>matrix: the uterus.</term> is a highly porous organ. Thus, after the fetus is formed, heat causes the male sperm to evaporate and withdraw from the womb, while the fetus receives nourishment through the pores. This is also evident because the womb is made of skin, and every skin in an animal is porous; otherwise, sweat could not exit without causing pain—which is clearly false, for the pores open in heat, and then sweat [exits]...

When there is a thick humor <term>humor: in medieval medicine, one of the four vital bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) that determined health and temperament</term> in the animal body that is harmful to it, nature diverts it to the external parts of the body, causing scabs on the hands and feet. Fourth, someone might wonder where the menstrual fluid comes from in a woman during intercourse with a man. It was stated above that when a woman conceives, the menses are retained; therefore, if they are being held back, it is surprising that they should flow during the act of intercourse. To this, it must be said that when a woman conceives, the menses are retained for a specific "final cause" <note>original: "causam finalem"; in Aristotelian philosophy, the ultimate purpose or "why" behind a natural process</note>: so that the fetus growing in the woman’s womb can be nourished by that retained fluid. 

However, when a woman engages in intercourse with a man, she experiences great pleasure because the nerves and veins within the vulva <note>original: "vulva"; used here by the author to refer to the female reproductive tract as a whole</note> are stimulated and moved by the presence of the male organ. Thus, through this dilation, the vulva emits fluid. This is natural in the context of intercourse, as the act itself is natural, yet it is, in a sense, "forced" <note>original: "violentus"; in a medieval scientific context, this refers to a movement triggered by an external force rather than the body's internal clock</note> compared to the regular, natural cycle of menstruation. 

Furthermore, from the nourishment consumed every day, matter is created that is naturally suited for expulsion during intercourse. This solves the doubt of why pregnant women often have a great appetite for intercourse. This desire exists because of an abundance of "superfluous matter" derived from food. Because the usual menses are being retained for the fetus, yet new matter is still generated daily, the woman feels a strong desire for intercourse; the abundance of this matter causes her vulva to grow warm, and thus she seeks physical union.

...[from the other] members. Natural heat <note>original: "calor naturalis"; in medieval science, this was a vital warmth inherent in living organisms that directed growth and digestion</note>, released in the man's sperm, and the heat of the womb work toward this milky color, so that this matter is whitened like milk. *This is the second chapter of the practical part, in which he returns to the formation of the fetus. A doubt arises: is the heat of the sperm an elemental fire, or is it a celestial heat? Similarly, one might ask about the heat of the womb, and so on. There are various opinions here, but following Aristotle in the second book of* On Animals, *it must be said that this heat is "animal" <note>original: "animalis"; meaning "animate" or "of the soul," rather than referring to beasts</note> or celestial. The reason is that elemental heat is destructive, but celestial heat preserves living things, according to Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to medieval European science</note> in his commentary on the 12th book of the* Metaphysics. *However, it should be said that this heat is partly fiery and partly animate or celestial. For fiery heat simply converts things into itself, as if into its opposite <note>like a campfire consuming wood and turning it into more fire/ash</note>. But animate or celestial heat is mixed with humidity and is tempered, and that heat preserves the mixture. <note>This verse refers to a popular medieval belief that four specific creatures lived solely on one element: the Salamander (fire), the Mole (earth), the Fish or Herring (water), and the Chameleon (air).</note>

It must be said that this is simply impossible according to Aristotle <note>referring to the Greek philosopher whose works on biology were the foundation of medieval science</note>. For instance, the herring <note>original: "halec"; here used as a general example of a creature in water</note> is a mixture of all four elements, and it is nourished by water that is already "mixed" with other substances through the mediation of the sun's heat. Thus, a herring cannot live in pure, distilled water because such water lacks nutritional value. This is why we see fish eat bread in the water. 

Furthermore, in every living mixture, **Earth** is required, which makes the mixture stable and hard; otherwise, the body would quickly dissolve. **Fire** is also required so that the body possesses the heat in which life is preserved. **Moisture** <note>representing the element of Water</note> is required as the medium in which that heat acts. Finally, the moisture of **Air** is required because the "spirit" <note>original: "spiritus"; in medieval medicine, this refers to a refined, vaporous substance in the blood that carries life force, not a ghost</note> is generated from aerial blood. 

In the same way, the **bones** are formed from the menstrual matter <note>original: "menstruo"; medieval thinkers believed the fetus was physically built from the mother's retained menstrual blood</note>—specifically from its coarser parts—because the bones preserve the human material in its being. If there were no bones, a human would quickly collapse or dissolve. Afterward, from the more watery parts of this same matter, the **brain** and **marrow** are generated. From the more "aerial" parts, the **spirits** are generated, and from the more fiery parts, the **liver** is formed. Thus, every limb in a human is constructed through the addition of a specific element. 

Note that the fetus is formed in such a way that the quantity of pre-existing matter is condensed or thinned out <note>original: "rarescit"; to become less dense</note> until it reaches the size and extension of its proper form: in length, width, and depth. [...Mars] gives the irascible power <note>original: *virtutem irascibilem*; in medieval psychology, this is the faculty of the soul responsible for anger, courage, and the drive to overcome obstacles</note>. The Sun is the best of the planets, influencing knowledge and memory. Whence those born under the Sun are happy and lovable. Likewise, the text states that an accident <term>accident: a philosophical term for a quality or property—like color, size, or an emotion—that can change without changing the fundamental nature of the thing it belongs to</term> is not supported within a simple essence <note>a "simple essence" refers to something like a pure spirit or the soul itself, which was thought to have no physical parts</note>. The reason for this is that an accident emerges from the nature of the subject, involving not only the scope of the subject (the "material cause") but also the scope of the "efficient cause" <note>The material cause is what a thing is made of; the efficient cause is the agent or force that brings it about.</note>. Therefore, the composite being <note>the human person, made of both soul and body</note> is the material cause according to one part and the efficient cause according to the other. Because these parts cannot be distinguished in a "simple" thing, a simple thing is not a subject for accidents—especially not "real" accidents—even though a simple essence could be the subject of its own "modes of being." This is similar to how primary matter is the subject of its own potentiality, which is its own proper and formal way of existing. From this, it is clear that the accidents of a person's powers do not belong to the soul alone, but are accidents of the whole composite being. However, they are attributed to the soul in this way because they exist in the body primarily through the soul's influence.

For particularly, something is produced in these lower regions by the causation of the higher bodies because one part of the heavens is naturally suited to introduce a specific and determined form, while another part introduces another form. # The Little Book of Albertus Magnus,

...[the first] month <note>original: "mus mensis," likely a fragment of "primus mensis" (the first month), as Saturn was traditionally associated with the first month of gestation</note> were attributed to Saturn, so that he reigned at the start of conception, then Saturn would always reign. I say that Saturn’s "reigning" is understood in two ways: one by general influence, and the other by special influence. Now, it is said that Saturn reigns every day through general influence; but the special rule of Saturn occurs when he is in his own "house" <note>In astrology, a "house" is a specific sign of the zodiac where a planet's power is most naturally at home</note>, and then he has a greater influence. 

Note that Saturn is cold and dry; therefore, he must influence the seed with moisture and heat, which are virtually contrary to him. Thus, all action occurs by virtue of contrariety <note>original: "gratia contrarietatis"</note>, because a thing added to something similar to itself does not act upon it. Hence, the agent <term>agent: the thing doing the acting</term> and the patient <term>patient: the thing being acted upon</term> are dissimilar at the start of the action, but at the end they are similar. This is because every natural agent assimilates its patient to itself as much as it can through its own power; for every natural agent acts upon its contrary to the limit of its power, as is clear in Book 2 of *On the Heavens* <note>Aristotle’s *De Caelo*, a foundational text for medieval science</note>. 

Note, the text mentions the "acts of active agents," etc. This is clear from manifest signs: for there is a certain common fish called a Scorpio <note>The Scorpion-fish (Scorpaena), believed in the Middle Ages to be able to numb a fisherman's hand even through the barrier of a net</note>; it infects the fisherman’s hand through the net, yet it does not infect the net itself, because the net is not "disposed" <term>disposition: the physical readiness or suitability of matter to receive a specific quality</term> for this effect. Likewise, the sun heats the air but does not heat the celestial orbs themselves—namely those lower than itself—even though they are closer to it. This is because of the "indisposition" of their matter. Therefore, those people have erred who say that anything can be made out of anything; for the first proper act must take place in its own matter that has been properly disposed for it.

Indeed, some add to this position by saying that the Sun is the root of all vital power, and the fourth month is assigned to such an operation.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of astrological influences on the human body, specifically why the sign of Aries (the Ram) governs the head. It addresses a scholarly debate between two great medieval authorities, Avicenna and Averroes, regarding the true seat of life—the brain versus the heart—before transitioning to the next zodiac sign, Taurus.</meta>

### Albertus Magnus' Little Book,

...in which all the powers of the soul thrive, precisely because **Aries** itself is the principle of vital activity; and thus the **head** is that in which all the powers of the soul thrive. For this reason, Doctors say that the **vegetative power** <term>vegetative power: the most basic level of the soul responsible for growth, nutrition, and reproduction</term> of the body is principally and distinctly in the head, but originates in the heart. 

However, there is a doubt whether life consists more in the heart than in the head. It would seem to be in the head, as is evident from **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard European textbook</note>, who says he saw a ram walking even after its heart had been removed; this could not happen unless life had its principle in the head. 

But against this is **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an Andalusian philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> in the sixth book of the *Physics*, who mocks Avicenna, saying that he himself saw a ram running here and there after its head had been cut off. Therefore, Averroes maintains that life is principally and originally in the heart, but exists in the head as a consequence. 

The Doctors are very much "sensualists" <note>meaning they rely heavily on what can be seen and felt via the physical senses</note>, and this is because they see that the instruments of the senses are located in the head; thus, they claim life consists principally in the head. But this is not so; rather, it is in the heart. 

What then shall we say to the author of this text, who claims the head is the most noble part of the body? It must be said that this is true according to outward appearance and the greater activity of the **vital spirits** <term>vital spirits: a refined substance thought to circulate through the body to enable movement and perception</term>, because the operations of life appear more clearly in the head than in the heart. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that nature placed the nobler and better part of the body in the very center of the body. For example: if two men were walking, and one traveled thirty miles in thirty days while the other traveled only one mile, then the one who walks one mile walks more quickly <note>This seems to be a logical or scribal paradox in the text; usually, the analogy explains that the one covering the larger distance in the same proportional time is not "slower," but simply has further to go</note>. # On the Secrets of Women.

->C 7<-

...nor are imperfect animals part of the perfection of the universe; however, they are not entirely in vain, because nature herself ordained that they absorb bad humors <note>original: "humores" — the four bodily fluids (blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm) which medieval medicine believed must be balanced for health</note>, so that humans might be better preserved from such harmful humors.

Whether these same animals are generated from seed or without seed is a matter of doubt among many. For the opinion of Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose works were central to medieval European medicine</note> in his book *On Floods* <note>original: "lib. de diluviis"</note> is that these same animals can be generated both from seed and without seed. He explains this by noting that a universal flood could still occur, and in such a flood, all living things would be destroyed. Once all living things were destroyed, celestial influences would act upon the corpses of the dead which have rotted; then, through the power of the heavens, the same creatures that existed before would be generated once more. Thus, one individual would be generated from rotted matter, and another, through the discharge <term>decisionem|the physiological "cutting off" or release of reproductive seed</term> of seed, would generate another like itself in species. Therefore, the same creatures are generated from seed and without seed.

He demonstrates the physical possibility of this by saying: if the hairs of a menstruating woman are taken and placed under rich earth where manure has lain during the winter, then in the spring or summer, when they grow warm from the heat of the Sun, a long and strong serpent will be generated. That serpent will subsequently generate its own kind in species through the discharge of seed. This same phenomenon is demonstrated in the mouse; for in its time, a certain mouse was made from decay <note>original: "putrefactione" — spontaneous generation from rotting matter</note>, and it subsequently generated its own kind in species from seed. Many more reasons could be brought forward, but the aforementioned are sufficient, as it would be tedious to narrate all the occurrences regarding this matter.

# Little Book of Albertus Magnus ,

Here the author raises a doubt. First, he presents the opinion of Avicenna and his reasons. Second, he briefly refutes it there. Concerning that opinion, note that Avicenna proposed a "Giver of Forms" <term>dator formarum|an external intelligence or agent in medieval philosophy that was believed to impart the "essence" or "soul" to physical matter to create a living being</term>, as noted by the Commentator <note>original: "per Commentatorem" — referring to Averroes (1126–1198), the influential Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> in the 12th and 4th books of *Metaphysics*. Therefore, he further proposed that divine power, through the movement of the planets, could infuse forms and grant existence. Then, from the decay <term>putrefactione|the process of rotting, which medieval science believed could spontaneously generate life</term> of things, creatures are generated, and both [the rotted matter and the new creature] generate things like themselves. For example, he posited that if the power of the sun produces a plant in the earth, that plant, by means of fruit and seed, could then produce another plant.

Note that the hairs of menstruating women are very moist, thick, and poisonous; therefore, if they are placed under rich earth in winter, moisture and poisonous qualities will be generated through the power of the sun, and they can be turned into snakes <note>This reflects a common medieval folk belief that organic matter, particularly when influenced by the perceived "toxicity" of menstruation, could spontaneously transform into vermin or serpents</note>. Thus, the basilisk <note>A legendary king of serpents said to kill with its gaze; here described as being birthed from an egg in manure</note> is said to be created artificially in manure from an egg. Manure is rich, fatty earth, filled with moisture, and therefore it causes things to bear fruit. In dry and parched earth, this is not true. In winter, manure is sufficiently moist and hot on the inside, because the surrounding cold does not allow the internal heat to evaporate or escape.

Note that a mouse generated from the decay of the earth is thicker than another mouse generated through the discharge <term>decisionem|the physiological release or "cutting off" of reproductive seed</term> of seed; it has a larger tail and is very poisonous, because the matter from which it was produced was highly rotted. Likewise, Avicenna posited that a certain calf fell from the sky, which he said had been generated in the air from decay.

### On the Secrets of Women

But briefly, it must be said regarding that opinion that it is not true. And the reason is that, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE), who was so central to medieval thought he was often called simply "the Philosopher"</note> in the 8th book of *Physics*, just as something has its own proper matter, so it has its own proper agent. This is because a specific form belongs to a specific matter, for the act of matter is one thing and the act of form is another, as stated in the 8th book of *Metaphysics*. And since those animals have different forms, they therefore have different matters, and consequently, they will have different agents and generating forces.

For the intention of the Philosopher in the 8th book of *Physics* is that the same animals—at least according to their species—could be created from seed and without seed, just as health is sometimes produced by art <note>Through the skill of a physician</note> and sometimes by nature. But in this he differs from Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were standard in medieval universities</note>, who says that "perfect" animals <term>animalia perfecta|complex organisms with developed organs and senses, as opposed to "imperfect" creatures like insects</term> are never created without seed; however, according to the Philosopher, this is not true.

He also differs from him because, according to the doctrine of the Philosopher in the 1st book of *Meteorology*, a universal flood <note>original: "Diluvium universale"</note> is naturally impossible, whether by fire or by water. And Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), the Dominican friar and scientist to whom this work is attributed</note> offers this reason: that a flood occurs due to a moistening constellation <note>The medieval belief that the alignment of stars and planets directly controlled the balance of elements (wet, dry, hot, cold) on Earth</note>. Therefore, if a moistening constellation faces one part of the earth, then the opposite side of the earth faces another, namely, a drying constellation. And as much as one part is moistened by the first, the other part is dried by the second; therefore, what Avicenna says is impossible.

*Here he rejects the opinion of Avicenna—but not the reasoning of the Commentator <note>Averroës (1126–1198), the Andalusian philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle</note>—by proving that the types generated from seed and those generated without seed differ in species, such that the agent is different and the recipient is different, whether they arise from propagation or from the decay <term>putredine|rotting or breaking down of organic matter, which was thought to release life-forming heat</term> of the generator.*

<summary>This page refutes Avicenna's theories on spontaneous generation and universal catastrophes, using Aristotelian logic to argue that different forms of life require specific types of matter and origins.</summary>

# Albertus Magnus’s Little Book

...[gene]rating; thus it is that the matter is different—namely seed [on one hand] and decay on the other, and so forth. Likewise, the active agents are twofold: such as the power of the Sun and the stars, whose heat is incorporated into decaying matter on one hand, and the agents from which seeds are released on the other—that is, in creatures produced through reproduction. Consequently, those two types of mice differ in species; and if a serpent is generated from hairs <note>original: "crinibus." There was a common medieval folk belief that horsehairs or human hairs left in water would spontaneously turn into snakes or eels</note> and another is generated through the shedding of seed, they differ in species.

Note that it is impossible for a universal flood <note>original: "diluvium universale"</note> to occur naturally, because the planets cannot align in such a way; however, a particular <term>diluvium particulare|a localized flood affecting a specific region rather than the entire world</term> can indeed occur. For instance, if all the "cold" planets <note>In medieval astrology, Saturn and the Moon were considered cold, while Jupiter and Venus were temperate</note> should meet in the cold sign of Pisces, because that sign is extremely cold, it could happen that a flood would then be generated in one specific region which that sign governs. Thus, a universal flood could not occur except by a miracle. For we read that a universal flood once occurred because of the wickedness of men, but that is not our concern here, since we are speaking from the perspective of natural science.

# The Little Book of Albertus Magnus

*Whether the pulsating spirit is a substance or an accident.* It must be said that it is a **substance**, because that spirit acts by means of the formative power; and because an agent does not produce a substance except by means of a spirit, it is therefore necessary that this spirit be a substance. This spirit is a <term>subtle body|In medieval science, a "subtle body" is a physical substance so refined—like a vapor or gas—that it acts as a bridge between the physical and the spiritual</term>, generated from the more refined part of matter by means of <term>putrefaction|Decay or rotting, which medieval scholars believed released the "vital heat" necessary to create new, lower forms of life like insects or mice</term>. 

But there is a doubt as to whether that spirit is animate <note>possessing a soul</note> or inanimate. It must be said that the spirit is not animate *formally*, but it is so *virtually*, because it effectively draws out the soul of a living being from that putrid matter. For this reason, <note>Avicenna (c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were foundational to university learning in the Middle Ages</note> Avicenna, in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, in that digression where he refutes <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), Plato, and Themistius were key philosophical authorities; here, the text joins the debate on how complex life can arise from non-living matter</note> Averroes, Plato, and Themistius, discusses how frogs are generated from putrefaction. 

However, the author says that the heat of the Sun attracts moisture from the putrefaction. I can prove this through experience: I take a "putrid mouse" <note>This likely refers to a mouse believed to have been spontaneously generated from decaying matter</note> and place it in a location where the Sun’s rays are at their full strength; I find that the heat of the Sun causes the entire "matter" of the mouse to exhale <note>to evaporate or turn into vapor</note>, so that nothing remains there except the skin. 

Note that in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, generation is divided thus: some is <term>univocal|The "standard" way of reproduction where like produces like, such as a human giving birth to a human</term>, and some is <term>equivocal|Spontaneous generation, where the cause and the result are different species, such as earth producing a mouse</term>. 

Equivocal generation occurs when the "generator" <note>the thing that causes the birth</note> and the "generated" <note>the offspring</note> differ formally in species—as when a mouse is generated from the earth, etc. Univocal generation is when the generator and the generated agree in species, as a human generates a human, or a horse a horse. From this, the saying of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics* is resolved, where he says: "Everything that is made is made from something similar in species." This is true regarding univocal generation, but not equivocal generation. Note that

The cause for the diversity of these animals is the division of the seed within the <term>womb|Latin: *matrix*. This method of generation in simple <note>original: *animalibus imperfectis*, referring to insects or small creatures</note> animals follows a similar pattern, insofar as there is something in that process that takes the place of the womb, and something that takes the place of the seed. Therefore, such moisture is divided through the locations where the fetus is brought forth within decaying matter, and thus animals are multiplied. The cause for the similarity among such animals is the similarity of the moisture drawn from the body into <term>homogeneous parts|Parts of a body that are uniform in substance, like flesh or bone, as opposed to complex organs</term>; meanwhile, the diverse species of such animals are determined by the opposite—namely, moisture drawn into heterogeneous parts.

From a **melancholic** nature, however, a narrow and short animal is generated, because the cold does not allow it to be extended, and the dryness does not allow it to be widened.

It should also be noted that the **choleric** type is usually saffron-yellow in color, the **sanguine** is red, the **melancholic** is black, and the **phlegmatic** is white. When their natures are mixed together, their quality and color will necessarily be mixed as well. ### On the Secrets of Women ###

It must be said that there is a twofold cause for this. First, if women's breasts <term>mammillae; the Latin term for breasts or nipples</term> were located lower down, they would impede their movement; therefore, wise nature ordained it so. But the cow, the goat, and other animals have four legs, and therefore their breasts do not impede their movement. The second cause is that in women, heat <term>calor; specifically "vital heat," which medieval science believed drove all biological processes</term> depends on the heart, and that heat extends itself as far as the breasts; therefore, they have them on the chest next to the heart. But in beasts, the heat depends mostly on the liver <note>original: "hepate"</note>, and therefore the heat flows to the breasts [located] below, and for this reason they are also more easily milked and suckled by their offspring.

But you may ask, why do men not have breasts? The reason is that men do not experience menstruation and do not nourish children; therefore, it is not necessary. However, they do have very small ones, just as women have very small testicles <note>original: "testiculos"; in medieval medicine, ovaries were viewed as internal versions of the male organs and were often called "female testicles."</note>. But you might ask, are small breasts better than large ones? It must be said that medium-sized ones are more effective, whereas large ones are not useful because in them the heat is diffused here and there; they do not possess much heat, and there the digestion <note>In this context, "digestion" refers to the biological "cooking" or processing of blood into milk.</note> is poor. Likewise, small ones are not effective because there is little nourishment in them.

Also note that the fetus in the mother's womb is disposed according to her nourishment; and therefore, pregnant women are forbidden from, and should beware of, very strong drink, such as strong wine. This is because they cannot properly digest <note>original: "digerrere"</note> that strong drink, and a strong drink is not suitable for the fetus, since the fetus itself is still very tender and weak.

### On Monsters in Nature.

### CHAPTER VI.

As Aristotle says in the second book of the *Physics*, just as there is error <note>original: "peccatum"; literally "sin," but used here in the Aristotelian sense of a failure or deviation in a natural process</note> in nature, so there is also in art. The explanation of this point is very useful for the present business and for making our intention clear, insofar as it is now helpful. Hence, it should be known that those individuals of any species who, in some part of the body, deviate from the common course of that species, are called monsters <note>original: "monstra"</note> or errors in nature. This is seen, for example, in humans who have only one foot, or only one hand, and so on with others.

It must be noted, however, that this marvel <note>original: "miraculum"; used here to mean an unusual or striking phenomenon</note>, which the Philosophers call a "monster of nature," happens in many ways: either from a deficiency of matter <term>materia; the physical substance from which the fetus is formed, specifically menstrual blood in medieval theory</term> or from a surplus.

Regarding deficiency, it occurs in several ways. In the first way, the deficiency is attributed to the matter itself. In such a case, when the principal members <term>membra principalia; the vital organs necessary for life, such as the heart, brain, and liver</term> must first be formed and organized in the child, wise and ingenious nature acts as completely as she can and forms those parts which are principal. Once these have been formed and arranged, she applies herself to the formation of the remaining members; and there, using whatever matter she has left, she does what she can. She forms a diminished part when there is a deficiency in the matter, and thus an error occurs. For this reason, it sometimes happens that the head is larger or smaller than nature requires for that particular individual thus generated...

### D 6

...because if the reduction in the matter that precedes the formation had not stood in the way, a head formed under such a reduction of matter would be proportional to the nature of the individual, both in itself and in all its other members. This same conclusion can be drawn regarding the other principal organs, since a specific order is owed to these principal organs, as natural philosophers and physicians testify. In another way, however, the reduction of matter is specifically attributed to some particular part that is to be generated.

*Here the author carries out his intention regarding the manner in which monsters are generated in nature, and he introduces a comparison. He argues that nature is like art <note>original: "ars"; in this context, "art" refers to craftsmanship or a technical skill like building</note>, because just as a craftsman first forms and builds a solid foundation and afterwards strives to build upon that foundation, so similarly nature first forms the principal and more necessary members—namely the heart, liver, brain, and testicles—and afterwards the less principal ones, such as the hands, feet, and arms. Thus, if there is a defect in the matter, it is better for the more principal parts to exist than the less principal ones.*

*Note that nature is twofold: one is the **intending nature** <term>natura intendens; the "blueprint" or the ideal design that nature aims to achieve</term>, and the other is the **producing nature** <term>natura producens; the actual physical process of growth and formation</term>. Now, the intending nature does not err, because it always intends what is best. But the producing nature sometimes errs, because it does not always achieve what is best; but this happens on the part of the matter being either abundant or deficient, so that monsters are created according to the defect of the matter. And this happens in two ways: either according to a discrete quantity—thus sometimes a person is generated with only one foot, or with four fingers on one hand.*

Likewise, monsters are also especially created through **celestial influences**, because sometimes a specific constellation reigns, and from it, diverse shapes are influenced. # Albert the Great's Little Book,

# The Booklet of Albertus Magnus

...in the discourse of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the influential Greco-Egyptian astronomer and astrologer.</note> he recounts various signs and miracles concerning the inscription or carving of stones.

I say, according to **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), whose philosophical works synthesized Aristotelian thought with Islamic theology.</note>, that it is not always possible on the part of **particular nature** <term>naturae particularis; the specific biological force within an individual organism</term> for all matter to be moved toward its proper end; nor should it be conceded that the **privations** <term>privationes; the absence or failure of a natural quality or action</term> of its actions have their own ends. Likewise, note that particular nature does not intend the ends of privations—for it sees that "to be" is better than "not to be"—but God and celestial nature know how to arrange all things for the best, and this is called the "unfailing intelligence." Hence, according to the first book of **On the Heavens** <note>Aristotle’s *De Caelo*, a fundamental text on cosmology</note>, all death, corruption, sickness, and infirmity are **beyond nature** <note>original: *praeter naturam*; occurring outside the normal or intended course of biological development</note>.*

## C H A P T E R VII.

Having finished our discourse, as much as is sufficient, regarding the generation and formation of the **fetus** <term>fœtus; the developing offspring in the womb</term>, and according to what manner it occurs and many other incidental matters. For if a woman, when she has been in intercourse with a man, feels cold after the act and pain in her legs, it is a sign that she has conceived. The second sign: if the woman emits little or no **seed** <note>original: *semen*; medieval scientists often believed both men and women contributed "seed" to conception, or that the lack of emission indicated the womb had closed to retain the material</note>, it is a sign that she has conceived.

And we see this in a similar case, because when a person eats, after this they suffer cold, because the natural heat passes to the stomach to transform the food. Also, salt placed upon the tips of the breasts <note>original: *mammillarum*</note>, if it does not melt, is a sign of a **male** child.

*The cause of this fourth sign is that the breasts are warm; therefore, that heat causes the salt to harden. Wherefore salt, by grace of heat, remains firm in its parts. Hence the heat of fire extracts the finer parts from the water and causes those parts to evaporate, and then the moister and thicker earthy parts remain there, and these harden through the heat. Hence in the fourth book of the **Metaphysics** <note>Though the text says *Metaphysics*, this reference is actually to Book IV of Aristotle’s *Meteorology*, which was the standard medieval textbook for the transformation of elements and properties like melting and hardening.</note> it is said: If salt is to be resolved into its matter and first form, it is resolved into water, and thus it dissolves. Therefore, if salt is placed near fire, it begins to break apart and jump <note>original: *salire*; the author is making a wordplay on *sal* (salt) and the verb *salire* (to jump or leap), describing the crackling of salt in a flame</note>, because it encounters its opposite.*

Another sign: if the woman first moves her **right foot**, it is a sign of a **male**. And it happens in the opposite way if a **female** has been conceived: then the woman is heavy and pale, the belly is elongated and rounded on the left, the breast on the left side becomes dark, and her milk will be black, unconcocted <term>indigestum; in medieval medicine, "digestion" or "concoction" refers to the process where internal heat matures bodily fluids like milk or blood</term>, bluish, and watery, and thin. If placed upon the body, its parts divide clearly, and if placed upon a spring or urine, it floats; and so it goes for the other signs. Also, if there is pain on the left side, it is always a female; if indeed on the right, it is a male. ### On the signs of the loss of virginity.

### CHAPTER 9.

Following this, one should note the signs of the loss of chastity. Regarding this, it should be observed that sometimes virgins are severely altered <note>original: *corrumpuntur*; literally "corrupted," a term used in medieval medicine to describe the physical loss of virginity or defloration</note>, such that their vulva is greatly widened because the male member <note>original: *membrum virile*; a standard anatomical term for the penis</note> was too large and ill-fitted. Thus, the woman acquires such a wide vulva that the man may perform intercourse without pain to his own member, and then she has been previously deflowered. This is the reason why young women feel pain in the vulva the first time they are deflowered: because it must be widened and prepared for intercourse. There is another contributing cause: because there is a certain thin membrane <note>original: *pellicula*; a reference to the hymen</note> in the vulva and bladder that is broken. And the more they engage in intercourse, the more they are strengthened in such a game <note>original: *ludo*; a common medieval euphemism for sexual activity</note>.

*The author here proceeds with the signs of lost chastity, and it is clear enough in the text. But outside of the main text, there is another sign: that a virgin’s vulva is always closed, but a woman's stands always open; therefore, a virgin urinates at a higher angle <note>literally "urinates higher"; a folk belief regarding the physical trajectory of the urine stream</note> than a woman. Note: if you wish to test whether a virgin has been deflowered, grind thoroughly the saffron-colored lily flowers <note>referring to the yellow anthers/pollen found inside the flower</note> that are found among the flowers, and give that powder to her to eat. If she has been deflowered, she will urinate immediately. Likewise, have her urinate in the morning upon a certain herb which is commonly called mallow (papel); if it becomes dry, then she has been deflowered. Or take the fruit of lettuce and place it before her nostrils; if she is then deflowered, she urinates immediately.*

### On the signs of chastity.

### CHAPTER 10.

The signs of chastity <note>original: *castitatis*; referring specifically to virginity</note> are these: modesty, shame, and fear, along with a chaste gait and speech, and behaving modestly in relation to men and their advances. If, however, it is golden in color, clear, and heavy, it contains a sign of a joyful spirit—that is, of sexual desire—and this is true in those who are not "corrupted" <note>original: *non corruptis*; a medieval medical term for those who have not had sexual intercourse</note>.

Therefore, everyone should take care not to have intercourse with them then, because it is harmful. For this reason, wise women know how to protect themselves then, and are separated from men during the time of the menstrual flow.

### THE FINAL CHAPTER.

Before we truly put an end to our words—so that our teaching may be understood with subtlety and more completely—since we have spoken somewhat about the matter of the <term>menses</term> <note>original: "menstruorum"; the monthly "flowers" or blood of a woman.</note>, we must now move on to the matter of the <term>sperm</term> <note>original: "spermatis"; in this context, the "seed" or reproductive fluid.</note> in man. Sperm, as was said above, is nothing other than the surplus of nourishment which is not absorbed into the substance of the body being fed. Regarding this, it should be noted that Physicians posit four "digestions" in a human being.

They say that the method of nutrition is such: first, the food chewed in the mouth is directed from the mouth to the stomach itself, and there the first digestion occurs. There, the pure earthy matter is separated from the impure earthy matter; that impure matter is directed to the bowels and is later emitted through the stool.

But the pure matter is directed further to the liver <note>original: "hepar"</note>, and there the second digestion occurs. And then, once again, the pure watery matter is separated from the impure watery matter. The impure watery matter is directed to the bladder and is later emitted through urination; but the pure matter is directed to the heart, and the third digestion occurs there, and the pure is separated from the impure. 

The impure matter is directed to the seminal vessels <note>original: "vasa seminalia"</note>, and from that comes the sperm in man and the menses in woman. But the pure matter is the blood, and that is directed from the heart through the large veins, which are called capillaries <note>original: "capillares"; literally "hair-like" vessels. Medieval medicine viewed these as the fine branches of the vascular system.</note>. Through these veins, the blood is directed to individual members <note>The various organs and parts of the body.</note>, and in those members the final digestion occurs, and again the pure is separated from the impure, and the impure is emitted...

Regarding this, it must be known that according to Aristotle in the fourth book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "4. The first operation of heat, in so far as it is heat, is to dissolve, evaporate, and gather together <term>homogeneous</term> <note>original: "homogenea"; things of the same kind or nature</note> things, and to separate <term>heterogeneous</term> <note>original: "heterogenea"; things of different kinds or natures</note> things. This second point is evident: for if a single mass of gold and silver is taken and placed in a fire, the heat causes the gold to flow away from the silver, and vice versa. And thus spoke the Philosopher <note>original: "Phil."; a standard medieval shorthand for Aristotle</note> in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption*, where he says that a specific heat acts like a tool—namely, like an axe or a double-bladed hatchet—which always dissolves things that are joined together.

But heat, in so far as it is <term>natural heat</term> <note>original: "calor naturalis"; the innate, life-giving warmth of a living being</note>, possesses within itself the <term>formative power</term> <note>original: "virtus formativa"</note> of each thing or nature of which it is said to be the natural heat. Thus, within it resides the "power of the heavens," or the power of the celestial movers, as well as the force of the seed, of the <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexionis"; the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) in an individual</note>, or of the form of that nature which it shapes. This can be seen in the heat of the seed of a plant or an animal, where there exists a force called the "form of the plant." In the same way, I believe that in natural things, natural heat directs the moisture, or the subject matter is proportioned to itself according to the requirements of each species. # The Book of Aggregation, or the Book of Secrets of ALBERTUS MAGNUS, concerning the <term>virtues</term> <note>In medieval natural philosophy, a "virtue" (virtus) refers to the inherent power, property, or "occult" medicinal effect a natural object possesses.</note> of Herbs, Stones, and certain Animals.

## BOOK FIRST

### *Concerning the virtues of certain Herbs.*

As the Philosopher <note>original: "Philosophus"; this refers to Aristotle, whose works formed the backbone of medieval science.</note> maintains in many places, all knowledge belongs to the category of good things. Nevertheless, it sometimes produces good results and sometimes evil, according to how that knowledge is applied... <note>original: "prout scientia mutatur"; implies that while the knowledge itself is neutral or good, its effects depend on the use to which it is put.</note>

## The Camel

The **Camel** is a well-enough known animal; it is called *Cyboi* by the Chaldeans and *Iphim* by the Greeks. ## The Hare

The **Hare** is a well-enough known animal; it is called *Veterellum* by the Chaldeans and *Onolosam* by the Greeks. And if it is given to a dog to eat along with the heart of a **weasel**, the dog will never bark again, even if it were being killed.

First, you will note that an hour is measured in two ways: namely, the **equal** and the **unequal**. 

An **equal hour** is the hour of the clock <note>original: *horologii*; refers to mechanical or standard 60-minute increments</note>, which is always of equal length. 

The **unequal hour**, however, is considered according to how the days lengthen or shorten throughout the seasons; for Astrologers always consider the time during which the Sun stands above their horizon, and they call that the "day" or the "diurnal arc" <note>original: *arcum diurnum*</note>, and conversely, the "night" for the time below. That time which they call "day," they divide into twelve equal parts, which are the [unequal] hours of such a day; and whatever is said regarding the day, you should understand in the opposite way regarding the night. 

And so that you may perceive this more clearly, let us suppose that the Sun rises above the horizon at the eighth hour of the clock <note>8:00 AM</note>, and we have until sunset 17 clock-hours <note>The Latin text says 17 hours, though the subsequent math suggests 16 hours</note>. We multiply these by 60—since there are 60 minutes in each clock-hour—and we will have nine hundred and sixty minutes <note>960 minutes divided by 60 equals 16 hours, suggesting a long summer day</note>. ...we will have 80 minutes for any given hour: therefore, such a [planetary] hour of the day will have 80 minutes, which comprise one hour and one-third of a clock hour <note>original: *horæ horologii*; the author is explaining that when daylight is long, a "planetary hour" is longer than a standard 60-minute hour</note>. *That there is within the souls of men a certain power of changing things, and that other things become obedient to it when the soul itself is carried away into a great excess of love or hatred for any of these things.*

Therefore, when the soul of someone is carried away into a great excess of some passion, it is found by manifest experiment that the soul itself binds things and alters them toward the very thing it desires; and for a long time, I did not believe it. But after I read books of Necromancy <note>original: *Necromantiæ*; here used broadly to mean forbidden or ceremonial magic</note> and books of images <note>original: *libros imaginum*; specialized texts on the creation of astrological talismans</note> and magic, I found that the disposition <note>original: *affectio*; the intense emotional or mental state</note> of the human soul is the greatest root of all these things—whether because it alters its own body and other things it encounters due to a great passion, or because other lowlier things obey it due to its innate dignity, or because a suitable hour or celestial order <note>original: *ordo cœleſtis*; the specific alignment of the stars and planets</note> coincides with such an extreme passion,

The method of the five characters <note>original: *characterum quinque*; these are specific magical sigils or symbols</note> is intended to follow a natural and probable path. When people see this happening among palms, they tie a rope from the male to the female. She then stands upright again, as if she has been harmonized with the male through the connection of the rope and the **power** <term>power: *virtute*; the innate essence or "virtue" of a natural object that allows it to exert influence</term> of the male.

...[the rope] with which a thief is hung, or has been hung, and a small amount of straw which a whirlwind has suspended in the air; if these are placed in a pot and mixed among other pots, it breaks all the others. <note>In medieval folklore, objects associated with death—especially the "thief's rope"—were thought to retain a violent or disruptive energy.</note>

**Likewise**, take a little of the aforementioned rope and place it in the peel <term>instrumento: specifically a baker's peel, the long shovel-like tool used to slide bread into an oven</term> with which bread is put into the oven; then he who must put the bread in the oven will not be able to do so, but it will jump back out.

**To make men appear without heads**: take a serpent’s slough <term>spolium serpentis: the shed skin of a snake</term>, orpiment <term>auripigmentum: a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment</term>, Greek pitch <note>original: *picem Graecam*, a type of rosin or resin</note>, rhapontic <note>original: *reuponticum*, likely Monk’s Rhubarb or a related medicinal root</note>, wax from new bees, and the blood of a donkey. **To make men appear to have the heads of any kind of animal**: take native sulfur <term>sulphur vivum: naturally occurring sulfur</term> and litharge <term>lethargirium: lead monoxide</term>. Having pulverized these together, sprinkle them into a lamp full of oil. Let there also be a candle made of virgin wax, which has been mixed with the dung <note>original: *fece*, referring to dregs or excrement</note> of that animal whose head you wish them to seem to have. Hold the candle lit by the fire of the lamp, and give them wine to drink with **valdimonia** <note>This likely refers to a mind-altering herb, perhaps a corruption of *vadimonia* or related to valerian, intended to induce hallucinations</note>; those who drink of it will see themselves as having the head of that animal.

**To make men appear to have the face of a dog**: take the fat from a dog’s ear and smear a little of it onto some new silk <term>bombycino: silk or fine cotton cloth</term>. Place it in a new lamp made of green glass, and place the lamp among the people; they will then perceive the face of a dog.
