**To make men appear to have three heads**: take the hairs of a dead donkey and make a small cord <term>funiculum: a thin rope or string</term>, and dry it; then take the marrow from the principal bone of the right shoulder <note>Sympathetic magic often specified the right side of the body to represent strength or dexterity.</note>, and mix it with a virgin branch <term>virga virginea: a fresh-growth branch, often of hazel, cut in a single stroke from a tree that has not yet borne fruit</term>, and smear the cord with it. Place this over the thresholds of the house. Those entering the house will appear to have three heads, while those who are already inside will appear as donkeys to those entering.

**If you wish for a man’s head to appear as the head of a donkey**: take some clippings <note>original: *segmine*, meaning shavings or skin-scrapings</note> from a small donkey and anoint the man on his head.

**If you wish for a chick or another object to jump on a dish**: take quicksilver <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the old name for mercury</term> and powder of calamite <note>original: *calamitæ*; this may refer to a loadstone (magnet) or a specific resin like styrax. In medieval magic, the combination of mercury and "calamite" was thought to create restless movement.</note>, and put it into a sealed glass vial. When you wish to appear completely on fire from head to foot, and yet not be harmed: take white **marshmallow** <term>malvaviscum: likely the common marshmallow plant (Althaea officinalis), known for its thick, mucilaginous sap which acts as a heat barrier</term>, prepare it with egg whites, then smear your body with it, and leave it until it is dried; then smear yourself with **alum** <term>alumen: a naturally occurring mineral salt used historically as a fire retardant</term>, and afterwards sprinkle fine sulfur over it. ...which, when it is lit, moves and walks: take the skin of a **wolf** and the skin of a **dog**, and make a **wick** <note>original: "lichinum"</note> from both, and light it with olive oil; it will immediately begin to move.

Philosophers say that the **crown of the head** <term>sinciput: the upper front part of the human skull</term> is the primary part of the head. From a human crown, a short time after death, worms are generated. When seven days have passed, those worms become flies, and after fourteen days, they become **great dragons** <note>This reflects the medieval theory of "spontaneous generation," where complex life was thought to emerge from decaying matter</note>. If one of these should bite a person, they will die immediately. *The Booklet of Albertus Magnus,*

<page-num>202</page-num>

If you wish to make all wonder cease, look to the other causes: namely, the **acting**, the **efficient** <term>causa efficiens: the primary source of change or the "trigger" that starts a process</term>, and the **patient** <term>causa patiens: the material or subject that is acted upon</term>; for if you consider both together, you will not be amazed. When you see such a great fitness in the sufficiency of one for the other, it does not cause wonder. For instance, when you see that cold water ignites fire and does not extinguish it, if you were to look only at the acting cause, you would always be amazed, because it would seem an efficient cause suited for this result. However, when you look at the **matter** of that effect—for example, because it is **lime** <note>original: "calx," specifically quicklime (calcium oxide), which reacts violently and produces heat when touched by water</note> and **sulfur**, which is highly flammable, so much so that even the smallest agent ignites it—you see that there is nothing wonderful about it.

Similarly, when a thing is consumed by fire, it is a wonder only when one of the causes is inspected in isolation. But when the nature of the **patient** <note>the material receiving the action</note> or the weakness of the agent is known, it is no wonder. Therefore, the greatest root of **natural experiments** lies in this: that they choose a material most prepared for a certain result, and either a weak or a very strong agent, or a material that is very poorly suited. Men likewise lead others to look only at that cause which does not seem capable of producing the effect, and they say nothing of the true cause. Take note of this: it is through this method that a multitude of wonderful experiments occurs. I will tell you some of these so that you may be confirmed in the power mentioned above, and so you may also learn how to devise the ingenuity of experiments yourself.

# MICHAEL SCOT’S
## Preface to the Secrets of Nature, as an investigator of natural things.

->To the Lord **FREDERICK**,<-
->**Emperor** of the Romans.<-

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut drop cap 'I' decorated with classical acanthus leaf scrolls and vine patterns.</image-desc>

EMPEROR, among the other matters which ought to occupy your concern is the knowledge of good and evil, and the investigation of this knowledge by every means yourself, through the books of authors and all branches of knowledge, and principally those sciences which are called the arts <term>arts: referring to the Liberal Arts, the core medieval curriculum consisting of the Trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and the Quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy)</term>. And you shall do these things thoroughly when your soul is at rest and your body has leisure, having set aside the business of the people seeking favors from your majesty or awaiting your replies. For you ought to know that there are two times for a living man: namely, a time of peace and a time of war; and likewise, there are two types of food, the physical and the spiritual. Physical food is prepared for the nourishment of the body, while spiritual food <note>original: "cibus spiritualis," here referring to intellectual and philosophical study as sustenance for the mind and soul</note> is for the nourishment of the soul. It must be understood that just as physical food preserves the body in good condition—provided it is prepared with reason and taken in moderation by the living being for whom it is suitable and at the proper time (since not all things are suitable at all times)—so too does spiritual food maintain one in a good state, if it is prepared with reason and taken in the due measure, at the proper time for both one's age and virtue...

It must be understood that the man is the active agent, while the woman is the passive recipient; <note>Scot is using the Aristotelian model of biology, where the male provides the "form" or "spark" and the female provides the "matter" or "nurture."</note> hence both possess a relative power, since a mutual relationship occurs during coitus. The lust of the man has its primary root in the loins, and the desire of the woman in the navel; as it says in the Book of Job: **His strength is in his loins, and his force is in the navel of his belly.** <note>original: "Virtus ejus in lumbis ejus, & fortitudo ejus in umbilico ventris." quoting Job 40:11 (Vulgate numbering). The suitable time for a man to engage in coitus is in winter and spring, but for a woman, it is in summer and autumn. This is because of the contrary <term>complexion</term> <note>A technical term in medieval medicine referring to the unique balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within an individual or a season.</note> of the seasons and the person. Thus, if the seed is spread lengthwise through the matrix, the fetus will be slender; if spread widthwise or in a sort of circle, it will be short and stout. ## CHAPTER VII.

Likewise, we speak concerning productive intercourse <note>original: "coïtu virtuoso." In medieval medicine, "virtue" often refers to the inherent power or effectiveness of a biological process.</note> and the generation of a creature, that a man ought not to have copulated recently, nor a woman, for a space of eight days. Truly, in conceiving, a woman ought not to be full of "flowers" <gloss>original: "floribus," a common medieval euphemism for menstruation</gloss>, nor entirely empty of them, but recently cleansed: so that the **womb** <term>womb <note>The Latin "matrix" is used here to refer to the uterus.</note></term> is somewhat clean. She should keep in mind someone beautiful <note>The theory of "maternal impression," where a mother's thoughts or sights at the moment of conception or during pregnancy could physically shape the child.</note>, so that the seed may run well into the chamber of the womb lengthwise, and the embryo may receive a form of commendable height.

...we say that it <note>Referring to the physical formation of the fetus described on the previous page.</note> is perfected in 70 days at the most, and in 65 at the minimum: hence, once its body is perfected, a <term>rational soul <note>original: "anima rationalis"; in medieval thought, this was the highest level of soul, unique to humans, allowing for reason and morality.</note></term> is given to it by God its creator, whom it entirely resembles. Hence, just as the body is newly created, so the soul is newly created and placed in the human body—and never in any other. For God gives a new and free soul to a new body, just as a father gives his son a new, polished, and spotless **tablet** <note>original: "tabula"; this refers to the concept of the *tabula rasa* or "blank slate," suggesting the soul begins without preconceived ideas.</note> so that he may learn with it. 1. Keeping it clean and spotless, a state which lasts for him until he has learned; but by being unwilling to learn, it is taken away from him in part.
So it is with the soul newly given to a new body: because it is, in a sense, within the body's own power, and its care is bound to the new body. With this soul, and through it, that same body can earn the praise of good works, by which it awaits the blessing of the eternal Father and the benevolence of the angels, etc. Likewise, it can earn the reproach of evil deeds, by which it awaits the curse of the eternal Father and the ill-will of the angels, etc. Thus, in a way, it is driven back by the anger of fury, falling into the hands of its enemies, who are the predators of souls that deceive and do not observe the commandments of God alone.

The second is the fault of the body, and not of the soul itself, since the body is not perfect except in terms of time, and not according to nature. # On the Secrets of Nature

From this, it follows that certain beings are born only once, such as man and the ox; some are born twice, such as birds and the majority of fish; and some are born three times, such as various kinds of animals like bees and butterflies <note>In medieval biology, the transformation from egg to larva to adult was often conceptualized as multiple "births."</note>. Indeed, a chick is born twice: first as an egg, and later as a chick, and so on.

Likewise, some animals are generated through <term>coitus: sexual intercourse</term>, such as man and the ox, while others are generated without intercourse, such as the eel, the crab, the scorpion, and others <note>This refers to the theory of "spontaneous generation," the ancient and medieval belief that some creatures arose from decaying matter or mud rather than reproduction.</note>. The fly and the frog do mate, yet they produce nothing <note>This reflects a common medieval misunderstanding of the reproductive cycles of insects and amphibians.</note>. Furthermore, among all those being born, some are born alive and with sight, such as man and the ox; some are born blind, such as the dog; some are born "dead," such as the bear <note>Original: "mortuus ut ursus"; it was a popular medieval belief that bear cubs were born as formless, lifeless lumps that the mother had to literally lick into shape.</note>; some are born as a mere piece of flesh, like the lion <note>Medieval bestiaries often claimed lion cubs were born dead or as formless meat and were brought to life on the third day by the father's breath or roar.</note>; some are born powerful, like the eagle and the majority of animals; and some are born powerless, like man.

It must be known that the blood of dogs and of infants aged two months or less undoubtedly cures leprosy when used in a warm water bath <note>This reflects the extreme and often gruesome medical "cures" suggested in medieval texts, where the purity of an infant's blood was thought to have miraculous healing properties.</note>. Regarding the love of the nurturer for the nurtured, and the nurtured for the nurse, we say this: that an infant who is raised in its own home, and primarily by its mother, is loved more by the parents and loves them more in return than one who is raised outside the home or by a foreign nurse. This is caused by the milk, the labor, and the habit of being together; hence, one who is well-nurtured at home and by the mother loves the mother more throughout their life. But one who is nurtured outside the home for a long time is, upon being brought back to the house, like a stranger compared to the other child—though this varies more or less according to how near or far away they were raised.

Why does a mother love a son more ardently than the father does, and why does she suffer more with his suffering, overlooking the offenses he commits against her? I answer that it is because she has more of her own flesh and blood in him, and she has maintained companionship and friendship with him longer and more closely by carrying him in her womb and nourishing him with her milk, and so forth.

Why does a father love a son more than the mother? <note>This question addresses specific cases of paternal preference, often linked to resemblance.</note> I answer that it is because the man’s <term>seed: semen, the formative principle in medieval biology believed to carry the "form" of the child</term> was more dominant in him, and the son is more similar to the father than to the mother. Why do a father and mother not maintain a "war" <note>original: "guerram," used here to mean a state of conflict or a long-term grudge.</note> against a son as firmly or as long as a son does against them? I answer that it is because he is their flesh and blood and not the reverse. Why do parents love the firstborn more than the others? I answer that it is because the experience is new; furthermore, if it were not a natural law that the small be loved so much, many would perish. I answer that it is because their entire "pledge" is held in him, and since they have no more than him, [their love is concentrated]. There are indeed many signs of a pregnant woman, some of which we shall describe in this place. Hence it should be known that when a woman has become pregnant, [it is not known] on that day except by the presumption of sexual intercourse having occurred; but before one month is completed, it can be sufficiently recognized by her and by others. ## *Probable signs, by which it is known to the eye and the intellect whether a woman is pregnant with a male or a female.*

### CHAPTER XVIII.

There are many signs, both general and specific, by which every wise man can judge whether a pregnant woman carries a male or a female in her womb, beyond those which we have stated above; and these are they. Place the milk of the pregnant woman into the palm of a hand that has first been cleaned; then press it between both palms, then open them and observe its state. For if it is thick in substance and not watery, it is a sign of a male. But if it is watery and not very sticky, then it is a sign of a female. Another method: let the milk be milked onto a mirror and allowed to dry there in the sun; if, when dried, it remains in a distinct bead <note>original: "in modum per se"</note>, it is likely a sign of a male. But if it is spread out across the surface when dried, it is a sign of a female. In <term>chiromancy: the art of palmistry or hand-reading</term> there is this experiment: have the pregnant woman show you whichever one of her hands you wish, and then observe the hand and her manner of showing it <note>original: "monstrum"</note>; if it is the right hand, it is a sign of a male, and the left is a sign of a female conceived.

### *How it may be known how many children each woman ought to have, once the first birth has been seen.*

## **C H A P T E R XIX.**

So that anyone might know how many children a woman is destined to have by observing her first birth, we say that when the infant comes out of its mother’s womb and falls down, and is lifted from that place by the <term>midwife: a woman skilled in assisting at childbirth</term> <note>original: "obstetricem"</note>, one must examine the nodes <note>likely referring to knots or bumps in the umbilical cord</note> of that umbilical cord <note>original: "umbilici"</note> which is attached to the <term>womb: the uterus or matrix</term> <note>original: "matrici"</note>. However many nodes there are, that is how many children <note>original: "filios"</note> she is still able to have and carry; for this reason, she shall have no more. But if there should be no nodes, it will be her own fault and not the man's if she does not conceive thereafter. It should be known that if a woman has no such node, she can produce no child within herself, even granted that she does everything correctly and follows all that is necessary for conception. Indeed, every time a woman gives birth, she loses one node, which falls off as often as she bears "the root" <note>this likely refers to the placenta or umbilical attachment</note>.

### CHAPTER XX.

# On the Secrets of Nature
<note>original: "De Secretis Naturæ". This text is part of a tradition of natural philosophy often attributed to Michael Scot, exploring how physical characteristics relate to an animal's inner nature.</note>

...divided in the legs. In animals there grow horns, hooves, hair, wool, **silk** <note>original: "sera", likely referring to bristles or silk-like fibers</note>, head-hair, feathers, scales, fat, marrow, and the spine. 

Likewise, certain animals live willingly in the society of their own kind: such as bees, cranes, doves, ants, birds, and so on. Others indeed are solitary, such as the scorpion and the spider. Likewise, some animals are prone to **frequent mating** <note>original: "multi coitus"</note>, such as man, the bird, the partridge, the dove, the rooster, the sparrow, and the fly. Likewise, some animals quickly receive instruction in **good manners** <note>meaning they are easily trained or domesticated</note>, such as humans, dogs, apes, and so on; some receive it slowly, such as the ox and the horse; and some never, such as the serpent, the frog, the fly, and so on. 

Some are peaceful and timid, like the sheep and the doe; some are simple, like the donkey; some are wise, like the horse and the dog; some are cunning, like the **dragon** <note>original: "draco", which in medieval texts could refer to a large snake or a mythical creature</note> and the serpent; some are deceitful in evil, like the fox, the wolf, and the scorpion; some are strong and bold, like the lion, the bear, the dragon, and the **greyhound** <note>original: "canis ligorius"</note>. Some are clever, like humans and apes; some are **modest** <note>original: "verecundia", implying a sense of shame or bashfulness</note>, like the goose and humans; some are shameless, like the frog, the fly, the donkey, and the pig. And some are swift, like the lion, the hare, and the deer; while others are indeed lazy, like the donkey and the pig.

### *Division of the chapter on animals.*
## CHAPTER XXII.

Every animal having lungs has a voice, and vice versa. Every animal having blood has a heart and a liver, and vice versa. Every animal lacking blood has a small body and is very fearful and weak—such as the fly, the gnat <note>original: "vibio"</note>, the crab, and the spider—and vice versa, as is evident in the case of man, the ox, the lion, and so on. Every animal lacking blood eats little, and vice versa. Every animal with long legs has a long neck: such as cranes, storks, and spoonbills <note>original: "cochales", likely referring to long-necked water birds like the spoonbill or perhaps a variant of "cochlearia"</note>; and vice versa: hens, sparrows, doves, and so on. 

Every animal that does not produce milk does not urinate <note>Medieval naturalists observed that birds and reptiles do not have a separate urinary tract like mammals, but rather a cloaca; they believed these animals did not "urinate" in the human sense</note>, such as the goose, the dove, and the hen; and vice versa, such as man, the ox, the sheep, and so on. Every animal lacking lungs lacks a throat and a neck; such as the fish, the crab, the grain-beetle <note>original: "graneus"</note>, the bedbug, and so on. Every animal lacking feet lacks a throat: such as the fish, the serpent, the slug <note>original: "ruxa", likely a regional term for a gastropod or soft-bodied crawler</note>, the earthworm, and the common worm. 

Every animal that lays eggs lacks a bladder, such as the hen, the peacock, and so on. Every animal that generates live young has a bladder, such as man and the pig; and vice versa <note>The author uses "e converso" here to indicate that those who do not bear live young, like the frog and the fly, lack these organs</note>, such as the frog and the fly. Every egg that is long and pointed at the ends produces a male offspring, and vice versa, such as the round egg <note>This was a common medieval belief regarding the sex of chicks based on egg shape</note>. Every egg with two yolks contains two chicks. 

Every animal that frequently releases its seed <note>refers to frequent mating or ejaculation</note> quickly grows gray: if it lives long, it quickly dies, afflicted by frequent exhaustion; yet it dies even more quickly if it does not release it at all, as is evident in the case of man in respect to woman <note>Medieval medicine taught that "retention of seed" could lead to toxic imbalances, particularly in men, who were considered to have a more "fiery" temperament that required regular venting</note>.

Returning now to the doctrine of <term>physiognomy: the ancient practice of judging a person's character or personality from their outward appearance, especially the face</term> in humans and beasts, we say that souls follow the body. In and of themselves, souls are not subject to the movements of the body in which they dwell for a certain span of temporal life, at the end of which they are separated, and the body remains. This is clearly seen in excessive movements caused by drunkenness from wine, or by love, or by sadness, labor, and sickness <note>The author suggests that while the soul is distinct, it is deeply affected by the physical states of the body it inhabits.</note>. The reason is that the body and soul are of a single composition, which is why they act and suffer together. It should be known that among all other animals, there is no creature more unsightly to behold when stripped of the adornment of others than man when he is naked, nor is any more destitute. For the beasts of the earth nourish him as long as he lives, as do the birds of the heaven, and so on. For example, the sun gives him light, the ox breaks and tills the earth for him and carries all his goods from place to place, the sheep gives him wool, the earth provides wood, the bird gives him feathers, etc. Indeed, there are many animals to which, by habit, many men and many women are likened because of beastly—

Such men are often spoken of and properly named by those who hate bestial habits, using this example: "See this Lion, this Pig, this Donkey, this Dog, this Fox, this Wolf." [Or likewise regarding status or character:] "this Emperor, this Abbot, this Monk, this Saint, this Angel." Likewise, you might hear someone called "that Lion," specifically because he roars like a lion and shouts loudly like a lion, and so it is with other similar comparisons.

There are, however, many signs of <term>physiognomy: the ancient practice of assessing a person's character or personality from their outer appearance</term> that are entirely common to both humans and other animals: such as fear, strength, boldness, joy, sadness, love, hatred, health, and sickness <note>The original Latin reads *ægriudo*, likely a printer's error for *ægritudo* (sickness).</note>.

And in a woman, the foot is a sign; for if her foot is long, narrow, and thin, it signifies a vulva that is long, narrow, and thin, and vice-versa. # On the Secrets of Nature.

...[is known] <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of how internal traits are revealed by external signs.</note> just as sight is through the eyes, and hearing through the ears. Thus, if anyone were to say, "such a person sees because he has eyes," he would be mocked, and likewise regarding an old man because of the obvious signs of old age. Birds are known by their feathers and claws, horses by their teeth, and goats by their eyes, and so on. 

Hence, if it is said, "The lion is a strong beast, the pig is unclean, the serpent is bold, the cat is timid," etc.—for if these and similar things were spoken by someone, they would not be considered "knowledge" <note>The author distinguishes between "common knowledge" (obvious observations) and "science" (expert analysis).</note>, because such signs are common and known to everyone; therefore, no one doubts them, just as they do not doubt what is seen or commonly heard. 

Likewise, we say that no man has ever truly seen a man who was entirely like a beast—though this is said of <term>apes: the author refers to "simiis," noting their human-like appearance</term>—but a man is likened to animals by a comparison of nature in certain aspects, as in the case of <term>monsters: in medieval science, a "monstrosity" was a biological marvel or birth defect that seemed to cross species lines</term>. Regarding these, I do not disagree; indeed, it is possible through art and through nature for a <term>hippocentaur: a mythical creature with the upper body of a man and the lower body of a horse</term> and a <term>minotaur: a creature with the head of a bull and the body of a man</term> to be created. 

Therefore, no one can <term>practice physiognomy: the pseudo-scientific study of a person's character or fortune based on their physical features</term> using only common signs or only specific signs; for though all men might be able to recognize these signs, they do not all possess them within themselves. For who doubts common signs, or those things which are unknown? And therefore, it is not fitting for a wise man to state a common sign in front of others—such as seeing a strong man and saying, based on experience, "that man is as strong as a lion." It is already well known that he is strong as a lion, and so on. For we must wisely determine all and singular things which properly grant the science of physiognomy,

# The Little Book of Michael Scot

...so that through this science, as we will state clearly in the following sections, any person may be able to gain the knowledge necessary to attain respect, honor, and a good reputation among all people, along with personal profit. For every detail that contributes to <term>physiognomy: the ancient practice of assessing a person's character or personality from their outer appearance</term> is found in the body’s movements—specifically its form or shape, the resemblance of its limbs to certain types, and also in its color, the lightness or heaviness of the gait, the posture, the voice, and so on. 

It must be understood, therefore, that among the parts of the human body to which the science of physiognomy properly pertains, some are "simple," such as the tongue and the liver. Others are "compound" <note>original: "compositum"</note> or complex, such as the foot and the hand. We shall describe how all these features exist and are arranged in every human being—treating only humans and not other animals—following the order of the chapters under their respective headings. We will speak on these matters as they appear to us, and as they appeared to others, such as <term>Hippocrates: the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</term>, <term>Galen: a prominent Roman physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</term>, and <term>Alminsor: a reference to the Persian physician Rhazes and his famous medical work dedicated to the ruler Al-Mansur</term>, all of whom have spoken sufficiently on the subject.

But before we arrive at the full purpose of our discourse, we state by way of special instruction that one must be very careful at all times to avoid meeting or keeping company with an "unfortunate" man <note>In the medieval worldview, physical deformities or missing limbs were often seen as outward signs of inward spiritual "misfortune" or bad omens.</note>. This is a work of the higher nature—as in a man who is lacking a limb, such as an eye or a hand, and so on. The reason is that any such person is rendered "unhappy," and by his own misfortune, he stands in the way of the fortunate man. This causes harm to many, which is hidden from the ignorant person, since he cannot weigh this danger except through the path of this teaching or through the experience of his own misfortune. For...

### *Signs of the complexion by reason of the color in the face.*

## C H A P T E R  X X V.

A white color in the face, or a dark color mixed as if with whiteness and bluish-gray—or even a gypsum-like or leaden color—naturally signifies a cold complexion. A red and ruddy color in the face, composed of whiteness with many freckles, signifies a hot complexion. A white color in the face accompanied by gentle movements and a mixture of redness signifies a temperate <note>meaning "balanced" or ideal</note> complexion. A bluish or leaden color in the skin and also in the fingernails signifies a bad and cold complexion.

### *Signs of the complexion by reason of the color of the body.*

## C H A P T E R  X X V I.

A body with white skin and dry flesh, having some or much red color in the appropriate places <note>Likely referring to the cheeks or joints.</note>, signifies the dominance of red choler <term>red choler: also known as yellow bile, associated with a fiery, ambitious, or irritable temperament</term>. A body thick in flesh, with white skin and suitably colored, signifies the dominance of blood <note>original: "dominium sanguinis"; this is the "sanguine" temperament, usually considered the most balanced and cheerful</note>. A body brown in color and thick in flesh, with a small amount of red color, signifies a dominance of blood mixed with melancholy <term>melancholy: also known as black bile, associated with a pensive, serious, or somber disposition</term>. A slender or lean body signifies the dominance of red choler. A medium body—that is, between lean and thick, and between white and brown—signifies the dominance of blood mixed with phlegm <term>phlegm: the humor associated with a calm, cool, or sometimes sluggish nature</term> and a little melancholy.

A body that feels very hot to the touch signifies a hot <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four "humors" that medieval science believed determined health and character</term>. A body that is felt to be more cold than hot signifies a cold complexion. A body that feels rough to the touch signifies a dry complexion. A body that feels soft to the touch signifies a moist complexion. A body that sweats often signifies a cold complexion <note>In medieval medicine, excessive sweating was sometimes seen as the body's attempt to expel superfluous "moistures" caused by a weak or cold internal heat.</note>. A body that is light and graceful in its gait signifies a good complexion. A body that is heavy and sluggish in its gait signifies a bad complexion.

### *Signs of a body of a hot complexion.*

## C H A P T E R  X X V I I.

Bodies that are naturally hot grow quickly and well, as is clearly seen in infants <note>In medieval medicine, infants were believed to possess a great deal of natural "vital heat," which fueled their rapid growth.</note>, and they either become fleshy or dried out. Their veins are not visible in certain places, their breathing is distinct, and their voice is firm, strong, and deep. In sexual intercourse <note>original: "coitu"</note> they are vigorous and have a strong appetite for it. They eat well, digest their food well, and have a strong physical bearing. They have an abundance of hair on the head and body in various places; this hair is partly thick and bristly <note>original: "ericii"; literally hedgehog-like or standing on end</note>, which happens because of the great heat of the heart, as is evident in the lion, the rooster, and similar animals.

---

### *Signs of a body of a cold complexion.*

## C H A P T E R  X X V I I I.

Bodies that are cold by nature grow slowly and become only slightly fleshy. Their veins appear prominent and large, while their breathing is shallow or almost hidden. The voice, when heard, is thin or sharp. In sexual intercourse they are weak and rarely have an appetite for it; they eat little, digest poorly, and have a weak physical bearing. Their skin is white or rosy in color. Their hair is straight and long, whether it be black or white, and it is fine in texture. They are easily frightened and terrified, and they are weak when it comes to manual labor.

### *Signs of a body of a moist temperament.*
#### C H A P T E R  X X I X.

Bodies that are naturally moist are soft and smooth in their flesh; their joints are hidden <note>Meaning the bones and tendons do not protrude or appear "knobby."</note> and possess little strength. For this reason, they can endure little labor; they are timid and fearful of almost everything, and they sleep poorly. They are often moved toward lust <note>original: "luxuriam"</note> and have little body hair. Their eyes are always watering. Their hair is straight and fine, and they possess a good intellect for learning.

### *Signs of a body of a dry temperament.*
#### C H A P T E R  X X X.

Bodies that are naturally dry feel rough to the touch; they are lean in flesh, yet strong and durable in labor. They eat with pleasure and in appropriate amounts, and the joints of their limbs are clearly visible. Their hair is thick, rough, and curly.

They become hungry at appropriate hours, rejoice with those who are happy, sleep their full sleep, feel light in spirit, and move with ease. ## *Signs of an imbalanced and unhealthy body.*
### C H A P T E R  X X X I I.

Imbalanced and unhealthy bodies are in every way unlike balanced and healthy bodies. Consequently, such people eat poorly and do not care to drink; they digest poorly and manage their affairs badly. They do not possess good wisdom at the appropriate times and do not fully join in with those who are rejoicing; rather, they are, as it were, saddened and remain sorrowful. They sleep their sleep poorly, feel heavy in themselves, walk with a heavy gait, and rarely or never sweat. They yawn often or sneeze, stretch their arms, and are either pale in the face or excessively flushed. Their five senses are weak; they cannot endure labor for long, they quickly forget things, they spit much, and they abound in superfluities <term>superfluitatibus</term> <note>In medieval physiology, "superfluities" refers to excess bodily fluids or waste products like mucus, which were thought to indicate an imbalance of the humors.</note> in their nostrils. They are lazy in almost everything, and sometimes their feet, hands, and eyes weep <note>original: "lachrymantur" – likely referring to swelling, edema, or discharge.</note>.

### C H A P T E R  X X X V.

If the **temperament** <term>complexio</term> <note>The "complexion" or temperament refers to the unique balance of the four primary qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—within an organ, which medieval doctors believed determined a person's health.</note> of the **liver** <term>hepar</term> is **hot**, it is recognized by the width of the veins and by dryness; the person’s urine is deeply colored, and eating hot foods is harmful because it causes inflammation. If the liver is of a **dry temperament**, it produces little blood, the whole body remains thin, the belly is slender, and there is very little color in the face.

Thus, we might say that the **heart** is the fountain and origin of innate heat; after it comes the **liver**, and after that are the other parts of the flesh and soft tissues <term>puppæ</term> <note>original: "puppæ" — refers to the fleshy or pulpy parts of the body</note>. The **brain** is colder and moister than all other parts of the body, acting as the opposite to the heat of the heart. Thus, one balances the other. 

**Fat** <term>adeps</term> is naturally colder and drier, consisting of a certain coagulated moisture. **Bone** is naturally hot and dry. **Marrow** is naturally hot and moist. All **cartilage**, **veins**, **nerves**, and the **outer membrane** <term>panniculus veternus</term> <note>literally "old membrane," referring to the fascia or connective tissue</note> are of a cold and dry nature; however, they are less so than bone, which has a tempered nature, especially the skin found in the palms of the hands.

**Glands** are cold and moist, as are all the organs that generate fluids <note>original: "lac" (milk), though the author includes other secretions here</note>, such as the **breasts** for milk, the **testicles** for sperm, and the organs for saliva and the **lungs**. 

**Flesh** varies greatly, because depending on the temperament of the specific limb, it may be hotter or less hot. Nevertheless, all fresh meat without salt is hot and moist, while salted meat is hot and dry; they vary, however, according to the location of the body part and the amount of salt used. ...quality, wherefore according to the truth, very lean meat makes one fat, and fat meat makes one lean <note>original: "caro bene macra impinguat & crassa macrat" — This reflects a medieval medical paradox: lean meat is easily converted into healthy flesh, while fatty meat was thought to ruin the appetite or "melt" the body's own fat through poor digestion</note>. Cheese is a poor food, whether fresh or salted; however, it is useful and pleasant when eaten after other foods, because when taken then, it aids digestion <note>This is the origin of the "cheese course" at the end of a meal, intended to "seal" the stomach</note>. ### *Signs of excessive blood.*

### CHAPTER XLI.

When blood is too abundant, an itching occurs almost everywhere in the flesh, and chiefly in the arms; a redness abounds in the face, and a sweetness is constantly felt in the mouth beyond what is usual. Blisters form in the mouth and on the lips, and certain burning sensations are felt in the chest, which we call <term>carbunculos</term> <note>original: "carbunculos" — literally "little coals." In this context, Scotus refers to internal inflammatory "burns" or severe heartburn rather than the modern skin infection known as a carbuncle</note>, because of which the person loses their appetite and their sleep. The urine is red and somewhat thick, the body grows fat, and foods taste good when eaten, from which the person desires, digests, and processes them well.

### *Signs of excessive Yellow Bile.*

### CHAPTER XLII.

When yellow bile <term>cholera</term> <note>original: "cholera" — In medieval medicine, this does not refer to the modern bacterial disease, but to "yellow bile," one of the four humors, characterized as hot and dry</note> is too abundant, a lemon-yellow color <term>color citrinus</term> appears in the face, along with bitterness in the mouth, roughness in the throat, great thirst, and little saliva. The tongue is dry and rough, the head often aches, and the mouth is dry and weak. The appetite is slow, and there is yellow or green vomit with much bitterness. The stool will be dry, hard, and sparse—as if burnt and foul-smelling—and passed with much labor. The urine is thin, lemon-yellow, fiery, and clear. There is much wakefulness and little sleep, the flesh is lean, and the heart is unstable.

### Signs of Phlegm.
### CHAPTER XLIII.

When phlegm is overly abundant, an excess of saliva occurs in the mouth, that is, a great deal of spit; if this is white and fluid, it is a good sign, but if it is viscous, it is bad. There is a lack of thirst, a moist mouth, and the throat and tongue feel soft; the person drinks rarely or never, except during lunch or dinner. The urine comes out white; the person is sluggish in movement and weak when working. Superfluities <note>original: "superfluitates" — excess bodily fluids or discharges</note> abound in the nose, the eyes feel heavy and sleepy, and sleep becomes long. The flesh everywhere is felt to be soft and loose <note>original: "lasciva" — in this medical context, it refers to flesh that lacks firmness or is overly relaxed, rather than the modern sense of "lascivious"</note>, the appetite is weak, small, and sour, and digestion is slow. In the face, the color is white without any reddish hue; the bowel movements are soft and of little heat <note>original: "paucæ frigiditatis" — reflecting the "cold" nature of the phlegmatic temperament</note>. In learning, the person is of "thick capacity" <note>dull-witted or slow to grasp new concepts</note>; the eyes often water, especially in the morning, and the hair and nails grow quickly.

### Signs of excessive melancholy.
### CHAPTER XLIV.

When melancholy reigns too much, there occurs a burning of the stomach <term>ardor stomachi</term> <note>heartburn or acid reflux</note>, a great deal of "dog-like appetite" <term>appetitus canini</term> <note>original: "appetitus canini" — an insatiable, ravenous hunger</note>, and a dark or dusky color in the face. The blood is black and thick, and the urine is black or somewhat reddish, tending slightly toward greenness or paleness. The body feels cold to the touch, the person is dull in labor, and the feet are cold. The heart is very suspicious, and the person is sad from over-thinking, easily angered, stubborn, and loves to remain in solitude; they consume little food and drink.

### *A brief doctrinal note.*

### CHAPTER XLV.

Nature does nothing in vain, and in each thing she always performs what is best; therefore, no quality in the body is idle. It should be known that from the time of their birth until old age, a person never ceases to dry out <note>The medieval view of aging was a process of losing "innate heat" and "radical moisture," effectively a slow desiccation</note>, being born only so that they may die. In a hot region, people are by nature short in their skin—as is evident with the Ethiopians—or perhaps reddish with a bit of whiteness intermixed. In their flesh they are dry and curly-haired, having hair that is coarse and rough. In a cold region, however, people are born tall, with skin that is very white and smooth; they are nearly hairless or have very little hair, and in their being they are long, white, and soft. Note that "region" is a manifold term, referring both to a province and to a woman's womb <note>original: "matrice"</note>. If both the province and the womb are hot, the creature is generated—and once generated, remains—dark or brown. If the region is cold, the person is made more or less white, according to the complexion <term>complexionem</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within an individual</note> of that region.

# On the Secrets of Nature.

### 281

...of the lunar cycle <note>original: "lunationis"</note>, because a boy sees one thing in his dreams, a young man another, an old man something else and in a different way, and a woman differently and other things according to her particular state. Likewise, a dream during the initial digestion of consumed food signifies either nothing at all or pertains to the past. A dream occurring while digestion is underway, but not yet complete, signifies present matters, even if they occur with interruptions. A dream occurring after the food has been fully digested signifies things entirely of the future.

For this reason, when someone dreams something while sleeping, and upon waking that dream seems strange and of great significance, and they wish to know its meaning, let them rise immediately and write it down. Alternatively, they should not sleep any longer on the side they were lying on when they had the dream; in this way, they will remember it during the day, unless they had many different dreams during a very long sleep. If, during the day, they have forgotten any part of that dream, let them rub the back of their head—where the faculty of memory <term>virtus memoriæ</term> <note>Medieval medical theory followed the "ventricular theory," which placed different mental faculties in specific areas of the brain; memory was believed to be stored in the posterior ventricle at the back of the skull</note> resides—and then, with the help of careful reflection <note>original: "praejudicationis auxilio"</note>, they will easily remember it.

Likewise, some dreams signify profit, some loss, some joy, some sadness, some sickness, some health, some war, some labor, some rest, and some are merely their own explanation. For example: when a person dreams at a time appropriate to their condition of catching a bird, it signifies profit; to lose a bird signifies loss; to weep signifies joy; to laugh signifies sadness; to want to run and be unable to signifies a hindrance; and so on for the rest.

# ON THE KNOWLEDGE
## *Of Auguries.*

### CHAPTER LVII.

Auguries <term>auguria</term> <note>Signs or omens used to predict the future, traditionally observed from the behavior of birds or other natural phenomena</note> are found mentioned in the canons of the Church <note>This likely refers to ecclesiastical laws that categorized or condemned various forms of divination while acknowledging their common practice</note>; nevertheless, we say that certain ones are received through encountering a person or another animal, or by hearing a voice. In this context, an augur <note>original: "augur, auguris," a practitioner of this skill</note> is a man or woman who, through such knowledge, points out future events; thus, they know and understand how to judge each specific thing in general through the signs of this science. 

Therefore, it should be known that some auguries signify a good outcome, some a bad outcome, and some a middle ground between the two. For there are certain noteworthy things by which auguries are properly considered, such as the sneezing of one who is yawning, encountering the flight of birds, the singing of birds, or a voice heard speaking regarding a proposed business matter, such as a preceding dream. From these signs, a human makes an augury for another human, just as other animals do—such as the eagle, the jackdaw <note>original: "cornicula," a small crow</note>, the night-raven <note>original: "nocticorax," often used for a night-owl or a specific water bird in medieval bestiaries</note>, the raven, the owl, the woodpecker, the cat, the dog, the pig, the horse, etc., as is held in the Book of Auguries. 

Likewise, some auguries occur from behind, some on the right, and some on the left; and since they are diverse in their arrangement, each of them is properly named and known by its own name for interpretation. However, we say that there are twelve auguries in number, following the likeness of the twelve signs of the heaven <note>the Zodiac</note>, and they are these: Ferneva, Ferve-

*Varium* <note>meaning "the changing" or "diverse" sign</note> is an augury when a person or a bird, in their journey or flight, passes across in front of you, coming from your right side and moving toward the left until it disappears. This is a good sign for your business.

*Confernova* is an augury when you first find a person or a bird walking or flying, and it settles itself down again before you on your right side while you are watching. This is a good sign for your business.

*Confervetus* is an augury when you first find or see a person or a bird settling itself down on your right side while you are watching. This is a bad sign for your business.

*Scismasarnova* is an augury when you see a person or a bird behind you, and it follows you and passes in front of you; and before it reaches you, or you reach it, somewhere...

Likewise, if two men should give two sneezes at almost the same moment—that is, each of them makes his own sneeze—then it is a good sign for him to carry out whatever he intended in a specific matter; thus, let him begin the business immediately. He will prosper in a voyage by sea for the sake of trade, and also by land. Two sneezes signify a good sign for him, and conversely for one or three [which are bad].

# HERE BEGINS

## The Third Part,

->*In which are contained the chapters on physiognomy* <term>physiognomy: the medieval science of judging a person's character or inner nature from their outward physical appearance</term> *specifically regarding both sexes, male and female.*<-

### CHAPTER 59.

RETURNING more fully to the specific parts of the bodies of both sexes—namely, man and woman—following the general course of almost any person in every state of their being, we say that physiognomy <note>original: "physionomia"</note> is an ingenious science of nature through which the inner quality <note>original: "virtus"; refers to the inherent power, character, or strength</note> of any living creature <note>original: "animalis"</note> is known. And since some of the body parts <note>original: "membrorum"</note> are simple, such as the tongue, the heart, etc., while others are composite <note>meaning made of multiple tissues or parts</note>, such as the eye, the nose, etc., we therefore say there are many signs that exist together, the dreams of which the wise offer judgment. Therefore, it must be understood that there is a manifold difference between man and woman, which falls under the judgment of the science called physiognomy. For this reason, the science is to be applied literally <note>original: "proprie"</note> in a man, and figuratively <note>original: "improprie"; meaning by extension or less strictly</note> in a woman. The reason for this is that man, in his entire composition, embodies this science more fully than woman, so that the knowledge of the rules <note>original: "canonum"; the established principles or standards of the discipline</note> may clearly appear...

Therefore, a great deal of skill must be applied to the comprehension of all things necessary for this study, through the power of gathering signs, before a judgment is rendered for either sex, should the occasion for judging someone arise.

For we see a man with a face very similar to a woman’s; when we have observed him wisely, we judge him accordingly, and we do the same for other parts of the body, such as the hands. We also see a woman whose face and physical form are carnally similar to a man’s, solely through the arrangement of her members—namely, in parts of the body that are quite distinct, such as the hands, etc., as well as the face. Should we judge her in the same way we can judge a man? Not at all, but differently, and with less certainty, because a woman’s complexion <term>complexion: in medieval medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which determined a person's physical health and character</term> is far removed from the pure reason and temperament of a man in all things, at least in the manner that is considered common. Indeed, of what is common, two parts are attributed to the man, and a third to the woman. 

Hence, wishing to maintain the order of all and each individual part of the limbs, we will now begin from the head. We will primarily place a rubric <note>original: "rubricam"; a heading or title, traditionally written in red ink</note> for each part of the human body and no other animal, so that our work may be easier for every reader. And having enumerated all the members individually from the top of the head to the soles of the feet, we shall finish this work with the help of God, who created all things from nothing.

## *On Hair.*

# C H A P T E R  L X.

Straight and flowing hair, white or pale in color, if it is thin and soft, signifies a person who is naturally timid at heart, weak in strength, peaceful in social circles, and everywhere agreeable and gentle. Coarse and bristly <note>original: "ericii"; literally "hedgehog-like," referring to hair that stands up stiffly like a hedgehog's spines</note> hair, if it is also short, signifies a person who is naturally strong, confident, bold, restless, vain, often deceptive, a lover of beautiful things, and more simple than wise, even if fortune favors him. One whose hair is mixed and curly signifies a person of a stubborn intellect, or of great simplicity, or perhaps both. One who has much hair upon the temples of the face and upon the forehead—to the extent that the forehead may be judged hairy—signifies a simple, vain, and lustful person, quick to believe others, rustic in both manners and speech, and of a coarse intellect. One whose hair is very bristly and stands upright, yet possesses a fine head of hair <note>original: "cæfarie"; usually referring to a thick or luxuriant head of hair</note> in its beauty, signifies a person who is very simple, bold, proud, of dull understanding, quick to anger, a liar, lustful, malicious, and presumptuous in doing evil. One whose hair at the corners of the forehead is very bristly and entirely raised (or at least a small portion of it), and whose forehead is high, signifies a person who is simple and partly malicious, yet with a certain shrewdness in his ways. One whose hair is thick...

## *On the Eyelashes.*

### C H A P T E R  L X I I.

Eyelashes <note>original: "cilia"; in medieval physiognomy, this term refers to the eyelids and the lashes, often describing their movement and shape</note> that are greatly arched and frequently raised high signify a man who is proud, high-spirited, vain, boastful, bold, threatening, a lover of beautiful things, and adaptable to both <note>likely meaning both good and evil circumstances</note>. One whose eyelashes are turned downwards when he speaks to another or looks at another, as if hiding beneath them, signifies a man who is very malicious or deceitful, a liar, a traitor, stingy, lazy, secretive, and a man of few words. One whose eyelashes are naturally folded downwards, as if without a curl, signifies a man who is unlearned, lazy, suspicious, stingy, envious, and in many matters easily a deceiver. One whose eyelashes are very short and white or leaden <note>original: "plumbea"; a dull, greyish color associated in medieval medicine with a phlegmatic or melancholic temperament</note> in color, signifies a man who is as if suited for all things, timid, easily and quickly believing another, and vice versa.

### C H A P T E R  L X I V.

Large eyes, that is, thick or bulging ones, signify a man who is frequently lazy, sometimes bold, envious, partly modest and partly unable to keep a secret, agreeable, not stingy, vain, prone to lying, easily angered, of poor memory, and of coarse wit and little understanding—possessing less wisdom than he believes himself to have.

One whose eyes bulge prominently outward signifies a man who is simple or foolish, having little modesty, somewhat generous, easily helpful, of coarse understanding and wit, and quickly changeable from one state of mind to another.

### CHAPTER LXVII.

## Concerning the Lips.

### CHAPTER LXVIII.

Lips of the mouth that are very thick or excessively turned outward signify a person who is more simple than wise, quick to believe what they are told, of coarse digestion <note>original: "grossi nutrimenti"; likely referring to a robust appetite or a constitution suited for heavy food</note>, and adaptable to both good and evil. One whose lips are suitably thin and not much turned outward signifies a person who is discreet, secretive in all things, shrewd, prone to anger <note>original: "iracundum"</note>, and of great natural talent. One whose lips are well-colored and more thin than thick signifies a person of good condition in all things, easily influenced toward either side, but more quickly drawn toward virtues than vices. One whose lips are not well-balanced in every respect, such that one is larger than the other, signifies a person who is more simple than wise, of coarse wit, slow intellect, and of varying fortune.

## Concerning the *Tongue.*
### CHAPTER LXX.

A tongue that is too quick to speak signifies a person who is more simple than wise, of coarse talent <note>original: "grossi ingenii"; suggesting a lack of refinement or intellectual sharpness</note>, poor understanding, quick to believe, and easily swayed toward either side <note>original: "facile convertibilem ad utraque"; meaning they are easily influenced toward either good or evil</note>. One whose tongue stutters while speaking signifies a person who is very simple, vain, unstable, prone to anger but quickly calmed, helpful, and weak. One whose tongue is very thick and rough signifies a person who is shrewd, malicious, appropriately helpful, vain, disdainful, secretive, a traitor, a gossip <term>novigerulum</term> <note>A "novigerulum" is a teller of news or a rumor-monger</note>, fearful, and suitably impious. One whose tongue is thin <note>original: "subtilis"; can also mean fine or delicate</note> signifies a person who is shrewd, talented, easily frightened, quick to believe, and easily swayed toward either side.

---

## Concerning the *Breath.*
### CHAPTER LXXI.

Much breath signifies a person of much spirit <note>In medieval physiology, "spirit" (spiritus) refers to the vital force or "animal spirits" that traveled through the body</note>, and vice versa. A deficiency of breath is twofold: it arises either from the smallness of the lungs or from a defect in the chest. Therefore, an animal of much breath is of great strength and a great drinker.

---

### On Laughter.

## CHAPTER LXXIII.

Laughter abounds in the mouth of fools who have a large spleen, and vice versa <note>original: "Risus abundat in ore stultorum"; a common medieval proverb derived from Ecclesiastes, here linked to the humoral theory that the spleen is the organ of laughter</note>. One whose mouth laughs easily signifies a man who is simple, vain, unstable, quick to believe, and of coarse talent and diet <note>original: "grossi... nutrimenti"; medieval science suggested that unrefined food led to an unrefined or "coarse" disposition</note>, servile, and unable to keep a secret. One whose mouth laughs rarely and briefly signifies a man who is stable, tenacious, shrewd, of clear intellect, secretive, faithful, and hard-working. One whose mouth is moved to laughter with difficulty signifies a man who is wise, very self-willed <note>original: "valde sui sensus"; meaning headstrong or independent-minded</note>, shrewd, talented, patient, tenacious, studious of his craft, irascible, and a supplanter <term>supplantaneum</term> <note>One who trips others up or undermines them, often through deceit</note>. One whose mouth laughs easily, and while laughing often coughs, or yawns, or twists his head, signifies a man who is fickle, envious, quick to believe, and easily swayed to either side. One whose mouth is twisted in laughter with the mockery of another signifies a man who is arrogant, false, tenacious, irascible, a liar, and something of a traitor.

### *On the Chin.*

### CHAPTER LXXIV.

A chin that is large and thick with much flesh signifies a man who is peaceful, of middling capacity, of coarse talent <note>original: "grossi ingenii"; in medieval physiognomy, "coarse" or "thick" talent suggested a lack of mental refinement or a slow-witted nature</note>, law-abiding, secretive, and easily turned one way or the other. 

One whose chin is sharp and suitably full of flesh signifies a man of good intellect, a noble heart, and of quite commendable upbringing <note>original: "laudabilis nutrimenti"; this term refers to "nourishment" in both a biological and moral sense, suggesting the person was well-raised and well-fed</note>. 

One whose chin is as if double, with a certain valley, signifies a man who is peaceful, of coarse talent, vain, quick to believe, suitably helpful to others, and very much a supplanter <term>supplantaneum</term> <note>One who trips others up or undermines them through trickery</note>, and secretive in his deeds. 

One whose chin is sharp and thin of flesh signifies a man who is daring, warlike, irascible, disdainful, timid, weak, and somewhat servile. 

One whose chin is hooked <note>original: "recurvum"</note>, while being strong in the joint of the jaws and thin of flesh so as to be sharp, signifies a man who is most wicked, simple, daring, proud, threatening, envious, stingy, deceitful, quickly provoked to anger, wrathful, a traitor, a thief, and a supplanter.

---

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the beard, transitioning from the timing of its growth to the physiological causes behind hair and its relationship to gendered humors. It maintains the previous page's focus on physiognomy—the practice of judging character from physical appearance.</meta>

<page-num>309</page-num>
<header>On the Secrets of Nature</header>

...beyond the male sex. And it should be known that such hairs are produced from the **superfluities of food** <note>original: "superfluitatibus ciborum"; in medieval medicine, "superfluities" were waste products or leftover materials from the body's digestion of food and "concoction" of humors</note>, the vapors of which ascend up to the parts of the jaws just as smoke rises to the openings of a chimney. And when these vapors no longer find open passages through which they can easily ascend further, they exit from there in the form of hairs, which are called the hairs of the beard. 

Almost all women lack a beard on their jaws. And it should be known that all the humors from which the beard is generated in men become in women the **menses** <note>original: "menstruum"</note>, which occurs for them by a certain passage and according to the movement of the moon’s age, sometimes once a month, and sometimes twice. The exit of this is said to be a flow or a superfluity. 

This indeed occurs when a woman is not pregnant and has passed the age of 11; and this menstrual fluid is sometimes transformed into **milk** within the breasts. It is true that these humors are so subtle and hot by nature that hairs sometimes arise from them on the jaws of a woman, specifically around the mouth where heat most abounds, and such a woman is said to be "bearded." 

It should be known that such a woman is very **lustful** <note>original: "luxuriosa"</note>, on account of her hot <term>complexion</term> <note>Complexion refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual</note>. She is therefore of a strong nature and of a masculine condition. 

On the other hand, a woman well-cleansed of hair, and especially around the mouth, is said according to <term>physiognomy</term> <note>The medieval science of interpreting a person's character or fate from their physical features</note> to be of a **good complexion**—namely, timid, fearful, modest, weak, mild, and obedient; and the bearded woman is the opposite.

If a man does not have any beard at all, it must be concluded that he is naturally without one, or he has not yet reached the age to grow one, or there is a specific internal cause preventing its emergence. A boy lacks a beard because his **nature** <note>original: "natura"; here referring to his biological constitution and vital heat</note> is not yet powerful enough, nor can the pores of his jaws be opened; the same is understood regarding a girl, who, instead of a beard, experiences the **menses** <note>original: "menstrui"</note> due to the influence of the moon. A man whose beard is well-ordered, well-composed, and thick with hair signifies a person of **good nature** and a rational disposition in all matters, according to the circumstances and his established habits; the opposite is true for those with sparse or messy beards. This is also evident in those who have a poorly formed beard, such as **eunuchs**; after they have lost both testicles, they are significantly transformed by nature from the character of men into the character of women.

### *On the ears.*

## CHAPTER LXXVII.

The **ear** <term>auris</term> belongs to man, while the **ear-flap** <term>auricula</term> belongs to other animals; likewise, the **nail** <term>unguis</term> belongs to man, and the **hoof** <term>ungula</term> <note>original: "ungula"; Scot is making a terminological distinction between human and animal anatomy common in medieval scholarship.</note> belongs to other animals. One whose ears are large and thick signifies a simple or dull person, lazy, of **coarse nourishment** <note>original: "grossi nutrimenti"; in medieval medicine, a diet of "heavy" or unrefined foods was thought to produce thick blood and a sluggish mind.</note>, of bad memory, and of **stony capacity** <note>original: "duræ capacitatis"; meaning someone who finds it very difficult to learn or "take in" new information.</note>. One whose ears are very small and thin signifies a man of good talent, intellect, and wisdom; one who is secretive, peaceful, shrewd, timid, **tight-fisted** <note>original: "tenacem"; often meaning stingy or greedy in this context.</note>, modest, vain, boastful, spirited, of good memory, and quite helpful to others. One whose ears are somewhat long—that is, beyond the common shape—or wide across, signifies a man who is bold, shameless, vain, lazy, foolish, helpful to others, capable of little work, and given to much eating.

## On the Throat.

### C A P. LXXIX.

A **white**, **thin**, or **thick throat** <note>original: "gula"; this refers specifically to the front part of the neck or the gullet area.</note> signifies a man who is boastful, vain, fearful, lustful, a ready liar, reasonably shrewd, prone to great anger, and long-resentful. One whose throat is thin and slender, and in which the veins are visible, signifies a man of bad luck, weak, timid, lazy, of **coarse nourishment** <note>original: "grossi nutrimenti"; in medieval medicine, a diet of "heavy" or unrefined foods was thought to produce thicker blood and a less refined, more sluggish character.</note>, gullible, and easily swayed toward either side of an issue.

## On the Neck.

### C A P. LXXX.

A **long neck** signifies that the feet will also be long and slender; it also indicates a man who is simple-minded, unable to keep a secret, timid, weak, envious, a liar, deceitful, **unteachable** <note>original: "indoctrinalem"; implying a person who is resistant to learning or lacks the capacity for education.</note>, and quickly swayed in any direction. One whose neck is **short** signifies a man who is shrewd, tenacious, deceitful, secretive, stable, discerning, quick-tempered, ingenious, of great intellect, reasonably strong, and a lover of peace, authority, and all things that inspire awe.

### *On the Shoulder Blades.*
#### CHAPTER LXXXI.

**Lean and small shoulder blades** <note>original: "spatulæ"; while literally "spatulas," in anatomical Latin of this period it refers to the scapulae or shoulder blades.</note> signify a man who is weak, timid, peaceful, capable of little labor, gullible, and easily swayed in all matters. One whose shoulder blades are **spaced out and thick** signifies a man who is strong, tenacious, faithful, of **coarse intellect and nourishment** <note>original: "grossi ingenii & nutrimenti"; suggesting a person whose mind and physical diet are unrefined or "heavy," leading to a sturdy but slow-witted nature.</note>, simple, capable of much labor, who eats enough and with pleasure, and remains at peace. One whose shoulder blades are **curved inward** signifies a man who is lazy, shrewd, secretive, ingenious, and **underhanded** <note>original: "supplantaneum"; literally "one who trips up others by the heel," implying a deceitful or undermining character.</note>. 

One whose shoulder blades are **smooth** <note>original: "abrasæ"; literally "scraped" or "shaved," referring to a flat or less prominent bone structure.</note> signifies a man who is simple, tenacious, hardworking, modest in all things (such as in speech and eating), peaceful, gullible, and easily swayed toward either side of an argument. One whose shoulder blades are **uneven**, such that one is larger than the other, signifies a man who is lazy, slow of understanding, of coarse intellect and nourishment, simple, **hard to teach** <note>original: "duræ capacitatis"; literally "of hard capacity," meaning a mind that is difficult to fill with knowledge.</note>, faithful, bold, tenacious, a traitor, false, and untrusting. One whose **tops of the shoulders** <note>original: "humeri spatularum"; the acromion or the highest point of the shoulder blade structure.</note> are very high-set signifies a man of an open lifestyle, yet envious, simple, vain, a liar, unstable, bold, shameless, and quarrelsome.

## On the Flesh.

### *On the Thigh.*
## CHAPTER LXXXIX.

A **thigh that is very thick with hair and well-bristled** <note>original: "ericiis"; literally "hedgehog-like," referring to coarse or prickly hair.</note> signifies a man who is lustful, strong in sexual intercourse, and his semen is effective for conception. One whose **thigh has sparse, thin, and long hairs** signifies a man who is appropriately chaste—that is, rarely lustful—and his semen is not particularly potent for conception. One whose **thigh is sparse or poorly formed** signifies a man who is weak, timid, rarely engages in intercourse, and is quickly changeable in his inclinations <note>original: "cito convertibilem ad utrumque"; implying a fickle or unstable nature.</note>.

### *On the Hips.*
## CHAPTER XC.

**Well-fleshed hips** signify a man who is strong, bold, and proud, as is evident in roosters and falcons; the opposite holds true for those with thin hips.

### *On the Knees.*
## CHAPTER XCI.

**Fat knees** signify a man who is timid, generous, vain, and capable of little labor. One whose **knees are lean** signifies a man who is strong, bold, tireless <note>original: "fatigiosum"; meaning one who can endure fatigue or is hardworking.</note>, secretive, and a good traveler.

## *On the Legs.*

### CHAPTER XCII.

A man’s **legs** <note>original: "crura"; specifically the lower legs or shins.</note> **have large calves at the back because he lacks a tail**. It should be known that Aristotle says in his *Book of Animals* <note>original: "libro animalium"; likely referring to Aristotle's *History of Animals*.</note>, that every animal lacking a large calf on its legs has a tail of some substance, such as hair, etc. One whose **legs are thick in bone and flesh, and hairy**, signifies a man who is strong, bold, shrewd, confident, but of dull wit <note>original: "grossi ingenii"; literally of "thick" or "coarse" intellect.</note>, lazy, slow, and of hard understanding. One whose **legs are slender and not very hairy**, signifies a man who is weak, timid, of good intellect, faithful, helpful, and rarely lustful. One whose **legs are entirely bare of hair**, signifies a man who is chaste, weak, and easily frightened. One whose **legs are very hairy**, signifies a man who is also hairy around the genitals, and who is lustful, robust, simple, and unstable, abounding in bad humors <note>In medieval medicine, "humors" were the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) that determined health and temperament.</note>.

## *On the Anklebones.*

### CHAPTER XCIII.

**Anklebones** <note>original: "claviculæ pedum"; literally "little keys of the feet," a common medieval term for the anklebones or malleoli.</note> **that are thick, fat, very strong, and prominent**, signify a man who is modest, timid, fearful, weak, capable of little labor, yet shrewd, faithful, and manageable. One whose **anklebones have very visible tendons and veins** <note>original: "nervos... & veniales"; the text likely means visible veins (venas), though "veniales" is written.</note>, signifies a man who is bold, strong, proud, and spirited.

### *On the Feet.*
### CHAPTER XCIV.

**Large feet**—that is, those that are thick in flesh, long in shape, and possess hard skin—signify a man who is simple, strong, of coarse nourishment <note>original: "grossi nutrimenti"; this likely refers to a person who consumes heavy, simple foods or has a robust but unrefined digestive system.</note>, of slow intellect, and vain. One whose **feet are slow, slender, lean, and of soft skin**, signifies a man of good intellect, lofty talent, and one who is timid, weak, sagacious, easily fatigued, capable of little labor, and quick to believe <note>original: "cito credentem"; meaning someone who is easily persuaded or gullible.</note>.

### *On the Nails.*
### CHAPTER XCV.

The term **nail** <note>original: "unguis"</note> belongs to man, whereas **hoof** or **claw** <note>original: "ungula"</note> belongs to any other animal. Thus, **slender nails of good color and long shape** signify a man of good condition regarding his health, and indicate that his mother, during the time of her pregnancy, did not eat very salty things, but rather those that were mild <note>original: "insipidas"; literally "tasteless" or "unsalted." Medieval medicine often linked a mother's cravings and diet directly to the physical formation of the fetus.</note>. The opposite is also true, as is evident in the nails of birds, which are rarely so when compared to others. One whose **nails are pale in color** signifies health, and so forth, unless they are of a dry nature, as is evident in the claws of hawks and falcons.

### *On the Heels.*
### CHAPTER XCVI.

**Heels of the feet that are small and lean** signify a man who is easily intimidated, fearful, and weak. One whose **heels are large and thick** signifies a man who is secretive, strong, bold,

## *On the Soles of the Feet.*
### CHAPTER XCVII.

The soles of the feet contain signs—similar to the lines <note>original: "vinculis"; literally "bonds" or "chains," here referring to the creases or "attachments" of the skin</note> of the hand—by which the entire fortune and misfortune, the life, the character, and the timing of events for a living being <note>original: "animalis"; Scot frequently uses this to refer to the human subject as a biological entity</note> can be easily known. This is sufficiently clear in the art called Chiromancy <term>Chiromancy: traditionally palmistry, though here Scot applies its principles of line-reading to the feet</term>, which we have fully mastered in our day, as we have Aeromancy <term>Aeromancy: divination by observing the air and atmospheric phenomena</term>, Pyromancy <term>Pyromancy: divination by fire</term>, and certain others. For among those signs, some signify good, some signify evil, and some fall doubtfully between the two. 

It should be known that many long furrows signify many obstacles in life, as well as toil, poverty, and misery. Short furrows, however, are worse in every degree. He whose skin on the soles is thick indicates a man who is strong and firm, whereas thin skin signifies one who is refined <note>original: "subtilem"; can mean thin, delicate, or mentally acute</note> but weak.

## *On the Steps of the Feet while Walking.*
### CHAPTER XCVIII.

If the steps taken while walking are slow and wide, they signify a man with a poor memory, a coarse wit, a clouded intellect, and a stingy nature; he is capable of little labor and does not easily believe everything he hears. He whose steps are fast and short signifies a man who is quick in his dealings, swift to imagine things, and of a delicate mental capacity. He whose steps are wide and irregular...

...not holding a straight path, these signify a simple man of coarse digestion <note>original: "grossi nutrimenti"; in medieval thought, "heavy nourishment" or thick humors were often associated with a lack of refinement or a crude constitution</note> and one who is cunning in evil, as is evident in the fox.

### *On the Movement of the Person.*
### CHAPTER XCIX.

A hasty movement of the person, when it ought to be reasonably firm—whether he speaks, sits, or stands on his feet—such as moving the hands, feet, or head when it is not necessary: this signifies an impure man, lacking in judgment <note>original: "indiscretum"; someone who lacks the ability to distinguish right from wrong or act with prudence</note>, evil-speaking, vain, unstable, untruthful, and not very faithful. He whose movement is rare when he speaks signifies a man well-suited for all things, such as one who is wise, steadfast, helpful, stable, and of good understanding. He whose movement is swift and without cause, either before or after [speaking], signifies a simple man of coarse intellect <note>original: "grossi ingenii"</note> and great malice. He whose movement is limping <note>original: "claudicus"; while it can mean a physical limp, here it refers to an uneven or hesitant gait</note> signifies a malicious man, a liar, false, envious, greedy for the possessions of others, and somewhat suited for everything to which another is moved or ought to be moved.

### *On the Humpbacked and the Scrofulous.*
### CHAPTER C.

A hump <note>original: "gibbus"</note>, that is, a swelling <term>struma: a swelling or tumor, often used in this period to describe goiters or scrofulous growths on the neck or back</term>, signifies a man who is shrewd, very clever, of poor memory, deceitful, and quite malicious. He whose hump is only in the front signifies a man of a double mind <note>original: "in animo duplicem"; duplicitous or deceitful</note>, and more simple than wise.
