### *On the Stature of a Person.*

## CHAPTER 101.

The stature of a person reveals much about them; thus, if the stature is tall and very straight, and more lean than fat, it signifies a man who is bold, cruel, proud, loud, vain-glorious, prone to harsh anger, stingy <note>original: "tenacem"; this term can imply someone who is tight-fisted with money or stubbornly holds onto a grudge</note>, extravagant, not quickly believing what he hears, often a liar, and malicious in many things. He whose stature is tall and suitably thick signifies a man who is strong, easily unfaithful, false, of coarse intellect <note>original: "grossi ingenii"; meaning a slow or unrefined mind</note>, stingy, ungrateful, and treacherous <note>original: "supplantaneum"; literally one who "trips another up by the heel"</note>. He whose stature is very tall, lean, and slender signifies a man who is foolish, vain, a liar, of coarse digestion <note>original: "grossi nutrimenti"; in medieval medicine, this suggests a body that produces thick, unrefined humors</note>, troublesome in pursuing his desires, quickly believing, weak, slow in action, and very set in his own ways. He whose stature is short and thick signifies a man who is vain, envious, suspicious, more simple than wise, of coarse intellect, and suitably subservient and trusting toward another, but of long-lasting anger. He whose stature is lean and short and very straight signifies a man who is naturally shrewd, clever, stingy, proud, bold, secretive, easily fatigued, vain-glorious, reasonably wise, of good understanding, and very treacherous. He whose stature is leaning forward—not because of old age, but by nature—signifies a man who is shrewd, secretive, dull-witted, of coarse digestion, severe, stingy, hardworking, of harsh anger, and not quickly believ-

#### *A Doctrinal Note.*

### CHAPTER 102.

When you see a man who is ruddy <note>original: "rubeum"; referring to red hair or a reddish complexion, often viewed with suspicion in medieval physiognomy</note>, faithful, tall, wise, fat, swift, lean, simple, good, beautiful, not boastful, poor, not envious, fair-skinned, wise, speaking with a nasal tone <note>original: "cum naso sonantem"</note>, well-spoken, industrious, not a liar, straight in posture, not reckless, not gullible, yet easily suffering loss, fair-skinned, not easily frightened, speaking with modest habits, not treacherous <note>original: "non supplantantem"; literally one who does not "trip others up by the heel"</note> and yet shrewd, not hot-blooded in the flesh and hairy on the legs and chin, and not often lustful, gesturing with his eye, not deceitful and lying and vain, not sneaky, well-skilled in his craft, practicing goodness, comfortably wealthy and not stingy toward the misery of another, truly poor, not pious and merciful <note>This list includes several contradictions, suggesting a person who defies their physical type.</note>, sickly, a merchant who is not a liar or a boaster of his own goods, a buyer who does not disparage the goods he wants in order to get a lower price, and one wishing to be good toward God, not an adversary in many things: Return special thanks to God alone and his mother, for then it is a divine operation against the common course of the nature of this transitory world.

### *The final chapter of the little book of physiognomy, in which the purpose of the individual chapters of this science is summarized.*

## C H A P T E R 103.

Physiognomy <note>The medieval science of judging a person's character or future based on their physical appearance.</note> requires you to wisely understand everything we have previously stated in each chapter concerning specific judgments. You must do this so that, when making a judgment, you do not rush anyone headlong into this science; for a judgment should not be based on only one of these features. Instead, every Physiognomist ought to cautiously gather within themselves the "testimonies" <note>original: "testimonia"; in this context, physical signs or evidence found on the body</note> of the entire body. These should be features that are not temporarily changed by some accident—such as a shift from health to health <note>original: "de sanitate in sanitatem"; this is likely a scribal error or OCR typo for "health to sickness" (infirmitatem), meaning the practitioner should look for permanent traits rather than temporary symptoms of illness</note>—and include the evidence of the eyes, forehead, nose, ears, teeth, and so on.

Since various pieces of evidence provide a judgment on the value of Physiognomy, one must always lean toward a universal view and the judgment of the majority of all the body parts, which we have described above in an orderly fashion. He who acts otherwise will easily fall into error. The reason is that every limb or member has certain judgments within itself, as is clear in the previous chapters; therefore, no person can be judged solely by one specific member, as one trait may contradict another. In such cases, the stronger evidence must overcome the weaker. Because the body parts are many, and each has its own interpretations, the chapters themselves are not in error even if a person does not perfectly match every single description we have given; rather, the traits will be seen to be greatly diversi...

<meta>catchword: ...fied (Latin: cari)</meta>

<vocab>Michael Scotus, Physiognomy, Chapter, Science, Judgment, Member/Limb, Testimonies</vocab>

<summary>This final chapter serves as a methodological warning, advising the reader to judge character based on the sum of all physical traits rather than a single feature, as different parts of the body may provide contradictory evidence.</summary>
<keywords>physiognomy, holistic judgment, physical traits, character analysis, Michael Scot, methodology, medieval science</keywords>

<meta>The word "cari" at the start of this page is the conclusion of the word "judicari" (to be judged) from the previous page.</meta>

...judged by the whole; for if it were otherwise, it would not be a fair 
assessment. The eyes have their own judgments, and a person 
on account of the eyes should be evaluated in this way. But what purpose 
would the other limbs serve? Therefore, since there are so many limbs, 
there are many diversities in a human being. And thus, no person 
falls under the judgment of a single limb, but of them all. 
Wherefore, the individual chapters [of this book] are to be investigated with 
discernment and combined. 
Furthermore, it must be believed that there are many "accidents" <note>original: "accidentia"; in medieval philosophy, these are external circumstances or temporary conditions that are not part of a person's essential nature, such as lifestyle or illness.</note> 
which truly loosen the certainty of a judgment when we wish to 
consider the truth of such matters in everyone—namely: 
the age of the person; the stage of life relative to the person; 
long residence in a place; long-standing habits of study; 
long-standing association with a certain company; 
an excessive dominance of the humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine health and character</term> 
within one's complexion <term>complexion: the specific balance of humors that forms a person’s temperament</term> 
beyond what is usual; accidental illness; violence; 
occurrences against nature; and the loss of 
any of the five natural senses. Wherefore, finally, 
with great diligence, all these things which we have 
mentioned above are to be observed in combination. 
And so, anyone delivering a judgment about the past 
will in no way err; and having not erred, they will not 
deceive, God willing. And let what we have 
stated regarding physiognomy be sufficient.
